#4080. The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#4079. PS5 Has Officially Crossed 100 Million Sales, Sony Confirms

The PS5 has now officially surpassed the 100 million sales milestone.

This news comes via Sony itself, which has just released newly updated figures for the current-gen console.

On the Sony Interactive Entertainment website, it states PS5 has sold "more than 100 million" units as of 10th November, 2026.

This means that, since the end of the last financial quarter (30th September 2026), Sony has shifted another 2.1 million machines.

It's taken slightly longer for PS5 to reach 100 million than its predecessor, the PS4, which was reportedly the fastest ever console to hit the milestone.

Given the many hurdles PS5 has contended with during its lifespan — launching amid the COVID-19 pandemic, shortages, hardware prices skyrocketing, etc. — it's quite remarkable it's managed to maintain such a healthy momentum.

It's possible this recent surge in PS5 sales is related to the imminent arrival of GTA 6, as well as the usual bump due to the approaching holiday season.

In any case, PS5 joins the list of consoles that have surpassed the milestone, and it's the fourth Sony home console to achieve it.

Sony also reports that PS5 is its most profitable generation ever, so all-in-all, it's been a very good generation for business.

The console still has a bit of time left before the inevitable PS6, which is expected to arrive within the next couple of years; whether Sony can keep the momentum going into the new generation remains to be seen.

Stephen has been part of the Push Square team for over six years, bringing boundless enthusiasm and a deep knowledge of video games to his role as Assistant Editor. Having grown up playing every PlayStation console to date, he's developed an eclectic taste, with particular passion for indie games, arcade racers, and puzzlers. He's also our go-to guy for Sonic-related matters, much to his delight/chagrin.

His role is to keep Sony successful, keeping investors and markets happy, grow the company, try and keep staff happy where possible, and generally leaving the company in a better place than when he took over to transition well to the next guy after him. That is the right thing for the head of a global multi-national.

He's not a creative guy, but doesn't need to be, he employs many people in the corporate ladder that are and knows making great games, or movies, that resonate with audiences will be good for business. Hence we have games like God of War: Laufey, Intergalactic, Kena: Scars of Kosmora all coming.

So why are they not just doing what they did before, why not just focus on single player narrative games for example.

History is littered with the corpses of companies that got too comfy doing just one thing, who didn't diversify, or get with the times and are now a footnote in history. Don't put all your eggs in one basket as the old saying goes. Hell, if Sony were still focusing on TVs and portable music players they would have gone under long ago, it was only by diversifying into Gaming, Movies and other areas that they are still around today.

Hence it's also his job - and those he trusts to advise around him - to try and read the future, perhaps the next 10 or more years, and try and position the company so that it doesn't end up like that. Pushing into live service - a massive gap in their gaming portfolio - TV and other things is their way of doing that. Testing out VR, Cloud and other technologies, even if it's just a foot in the door, to make sure they don't get blind sighted and miss out on the next big thing. It won't always work, predicting the future is a fickle business, but it's also the right thing to do. I think the way they handled the live service push was poor, but it was also the right thing to do, from a business perspective.

I know it's easy to point fingers and attribute blame when things aren't going as we would like them to, but it's a hard role. I once ran a company with around 50 people and that was hard and stressful enough, Sony has around 100,000 employees globally, thousands of investors, shareholders and of course millions of consumers to all try and keep happy at the same time, never easy at the best of times.

And it's certainly not the best of times. The global gaming industry has taken a massive downturn post covid with a lack of outside investment and many global events all leading mass layoffs and studio closures. I feel it's far too easy to point the finger and try and attribute blame, and while there may be some to go around I think the reality is more that virtually every gaming company has had to lay off a lot of staff, especially in countries where PlayStation has studios where the cost of living and doing business has gone sky high. It's important to realise this isn't a Sony only thing. Hence, while probably an unpopular opinion among gamers, I think they have done OK to weather this storm. But then most gamers have probably never run a business and employed staff in tough times. Personally I think it could have been a lot worse.

#4078. Forza Horizon 6 explodes on Steam even before it's officially out

Forza Horizon 6 looks to have easily delivered the most successful launch for any game in the series on PC, with record-breaking player numbers.

Steam is abuzz this week with a couple of long-anticipated launches, but in Forza Horizon 6’s case, at least, the game isn’t even out for what will be most of its players. The anticipated sequel in the open-world driving game series doesn’t officially launch until May 19, but owners of its most expensive version - the Premium Edition - can play it right now.

That version of the game includes more than just a few days of early access, of course, but you’d think the $120 price tag would’ve only been palatable to a small group of players. Not the case with this game.

Forza Horizon 6, which has spent 16 weeks in Steam’s global top sellers list, currently occupies the number two spot, having jumped up three spots this week in anticipation of the launch. The game has also naturally been popular with players, so popular in fact that it has already overtaken the player counts of all other Horizon games on the platform.

At the time of writing, the game has peaked at 128,157 concurrent players on Steam alone (via SteamDB). The figure has already climbed several times during the writing of this story, so you can only imagine how much higher it’s going to get deeper into the weekend.

All of that, of course, days before the official launch on Tuesday, when, theoretically, the majority of the game’s audience will be able to start playing. In just a few short hours, Horizon 6 has already gone well above Forza Horizon 5’s peak concurrent of 81,096, as well as Forza Horizon 4’s peak 75,689 players.

Steam is the only platform that publishes player numbers, of course, but it’s easy to see how similar the enthusiasm is going to be on Xbox. Though the game is not yet part of the Game Pass line-up, those who don’t want to wait could buy the Premium Edition Upgrade to get the included content, and play it right now.

Game Pass, and Xbox / Windows Store numbers don’t factor into Steam’s, which is another thing to consider when viewing the numbers holistically. Indeed, given how successful Forza Horizon 5 has been on PlayStation 5, Horizon 6’s upcoming release on Sony's console is bound to be even bigger.

Forza Horizon 5 has been off to a similarly flying start in the first few days of its own advanced access launch, so it’s obviously not surprising to see Horizon 6 do better there. In case you missed it, check out our review of Forza Horizon 6. In short, we really liked it, even if we expected more.

#4077. "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

Shift Up CTO DongKi Lee, best known for his work on Stellar Blade and the studio's mobile games, recently spoke at a developer panel about his excitement to get hands-on with Xbox Project Helix development kits. All whilst in front of a senior official of team Xbox.

As Inven Global puts it, Lee was one of five panellists, comprised of execs from other development studios, and answered questions on what it's like developing games for console in the Korean gaming industry.

When asked about what advantages the console platforms have compared to PC, fellow panellist and former Tekken CEO Katsuhiro Harada took the opportunity to throw some shade at the Xbox Series S, jesting "I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released", attributing additional development resources to optimising games for the lower spec console.

In response to this, the Shift Up CTO spoke about his excitement to work alongside Xbox and his eagerness to see Project Helix developer kits in Korea:

"Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox 'Helix'. From an engineer's standpoint, if you provide us with a dev kit first in Korea as early as possible, we will put in our best efforts to develop for it."

Xbox players have been asking for a Stellar Blade port for quite some time, regularly mocking up fake Xbox Series box art and posting it to socials, and usually asking when Shift Up will bring the game to Microsoft hardware. #4075. Danganronpa Creator Says Physical Game Production Is Reliant On Day-One Patches

"We barely pass platform certification requirements"

Kazutaka Kodaka, creator of Danganronpa and The Hundred Line, has made a pretty incredible admission regarding the production of physical games.

His comments were made during a roundtable discussion at the SKY31 Convention Seoul (thanks, Kotaku) during which he explains how developer Too Kyo Games is able to meet ongoing demand for physical games, particularly in Japan.

Essentially, the production of physical games requires the original master to be submitted much earlier than digital titles. This is to account for the extended time required to pack the items, especially if it's a collector's edition.

So Kodaka-san confessed that the studio often submits builds that, in his words, shouldn't be played by anyone. He operates under the assumption that everyone has access to the internet these days and is therefore able to download a day-one patch to bring the game up to an acceptable standard.

“Honestly, we approach it with the mindset of finalizing the master via patches. Collector’s editions in North America or Europe take an enormous amount of time to pack with figures, so the master submission deadline is absurdly early.

"To be frank, we sometimes submit builds where we think, ‘No one should ever play it in this state.’ We barely pass platform certification requirements and release it while believing no one plays games without an internet connection these days.”

He goes on to jokingly say "I’m not sure if I should be making such risky confessions in a venue like this". To be fair though, it sounds like Kodaka is merely being honest and open about a practice that is widely adopted by the industry at large.

Hell, even Ocarina of Time received a day-one patch. Granted, this was primarily to enable connection to Zelda Notes, but if you bought the physical and couldn't update it for whatever reason, you wouldn't be able to use this feature.

Kodaka's next project is Danganronpa 2x2 for the Switch and Switch 2. In somewhat related news, it was revealed earlier this year that the collector's editions on Switch 2 would no longer come with a full cartridge, with Spike Chunsoft instead opting for a Game-Key Card.

#4074. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.3 will take us deeper into the World in Canvas and make Mortenax Blade playable

Honkai: Star Rail's next big outing will see the continuation of the Planarcadia story, and it's going to be with us soon.

HoYoverse has today delivered full details on the next major update for Honkai: Star Rail. Version 4.3, dubbed The Lethe Below the Living, will be available for all players on June 1. The upcoming update adds a new chapter to the Planarcadia arc, and introduce a new playable character.

The new narrative chapter will also unveil more about Mortenax Blade, the Trailblazer themselves, and the husk of the Aeon.

Mortenax Blade is the hero of this chapter, and he’s going to step into the World in Canvas. The goal is to - by borrowing the power of Voracity - excise Shuhu from his body and end the curse.

The Trailblazer goes on a trip of their own in Version 4.3, this time to Inkford Hermitage, right on the edge between the World in Canvas and the real world. They’re going to undertake this journey to warn Graphia of the Asat Pramad threat.

In case you hadn’t already guessed, Mortenax Blade is this version’s new playable character. The 5-Star Fire-Type swordsman is on the Path of Nihility. Blade’s Ultimate allows him to enter an enhanced state by deploying a special Bounded Field.

While the field is active, all enemies receive more DMG. Entering this state is also how Blade unlocks his skill, which uses a Sword Formation to deal more damage. This is then used to essentially unlock a second, more powerful Ultimate for him.

The benefits of Mortenax Blade’s kit extend to his teammates, too. Any ally who attacks an enemy with him on the team, they inflict a debuff on them. This also builds up a special Charge that Blade can later use with his Skill.

Version 4.3’s launch arrives alongside the Gift of Tempered Blade event. Through it, you can claim a new Trailblazer Outfit piece for free, but only after getting Mortenax Blade from Warping. The first phase’s rerun will be Yao Guang, and the second phase will bring back both Cyrene and Phainon.

You can also expect the Wispae Amusement Park to arrive within the World in Canvas, which you’ll get to design. You can plan where the rides will go, pick the different themes, set visitor routes and more.

Starward Mode is another new addition, which can be found in Memory of Chaos, Pure Fiction, and Apocalyptic Shadow. Starward will see you take on three different stages, which you’ll need three teams for. Clearing each challenge with full stars will reward you 100 Stellar Jades extra per chase.

There’s more coming down the line, too. A new Fate/Stay Night [Unlimited Blade Works] collaboration will arrive in a content up this summer. The event will give players a chance to earn Gilgamesh or Archer for free by logging in.

#4073. Ubisoft are reportedly tapped as one potential company that could acquire Arkane, though the Dishonored studio's own management may be in the running too

I'd really like it if it weren't Ubisoft though

Things are potentially looking up for Arkane, depending on how you feel about Ubisoft (and depending on who actually ends up acquiring them). I mention the Assassin's Creed developer because, reportedly, they're interested in buying the studio from Microsoft, having even made a bid for it. I'll go out on a limb here and say it's the whole being French thing, but uh, I'd really rather someone else bought Arkane.

This comes from, you guessed it, Bloomberg, who say that sources they've spoken with claim two other gaming companies have also made a bit. There is even the potential that Arkane would be sold to their own management, as Xbox are considering such a move. But overall, it doesn't yet sound like anything is leaning any particular way, as Xbox haven't formalised a deal with any of the potential buyers. Bloomberg also note that if a deal is made, this should then allow Arkane to finish their work on their Blade game, which is expected to release within the next couple of years.

Apparently an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg that the gaming company is exploring their options ahead of their December deadline, but didn't comment any further. Ubisoft reportedly did not have a comment to make on the matter. For some context on that December deadline, because of French labour laws, companies that have over 1000 staff members are required to search for a buyer for three months before they can just completely shut down. That makes December 13th the final date that such a deal has to be made by, meaning there's about a month and a half left to go.

Arkane's sale comes as part of a sweeping range of cuts, sales and closures being made by Microsoft at the moment. In July, it was announced that studios like Double Fine, Undead Labs and Compulsion would no longer be a part of Xbox, with all three going indie; Ninja Theory was also announced as part of these cuts, but unfortunately it's looking like they'll be shutting their doors. Thousands of Xbox staff were also laid off at this time, with more laid off in September, and even more coming this month and January reportedly. As always, solidarity with all workers affected by Microsoft's heartless and money hungry cuts.

#4071. "An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process," Nexus Mods say as they rule out barring generated creations from their site

"We drew the line where the real argument is"

The owners of Nexus Mods have ruled out instituting an outright ban on AI-generated works being uploaded the site, instead opting to expand their current rules on modders disclosing how they've used AI in making their mods. This latest move to address the waves of AI-created or AI-thumbnailed mods now hitting Nexus Mods on a daily basis follows Nexus' modus operandi up to this point, which has been simply to try and ensure AI usage is clearly labelled so prospective downloaders can make informed decisions.

"We won't introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods," Nexus Mods owner and CEO Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann wrote in a news post. "You may ask me why, since that is not the solution some of you were looking for. The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process, but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.

"This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct. Mod Authors should have a chance to decide about the further use of their work, and you should be able to decide for yourselves how much AI-based content you want to see, whether more, less, or no content at all.

"As for our own position: Nexus Mods will not use your mods to train AI and will not sell or license them to anyone doing so. We refused to do that in the past, and we will refuse to do so in the future. Given such a variety of opinions within our community, not everyone will agree with any decision taken. These are the ones we believe are right for Nexus Mods today, and we’ll keep adjusting them as the tools evolve and as we see how these changes work in practice, with your feedback guiding that."

In terms of the changes which are being brought in to toughen up the site's current three tag system design to make mods containing AI-generated content, AI media, or made with AI assistance easier to spot, Nexus are making AI disclosures mandatory for those uploading new mods. "What this means is that for mods tagged as AI-assisted, we’re also introducing a requirement for a public explanation of how and where AI was used, which should give you a better understanding of what you’re downloading, rather than leaving you to make assumptions on a tag alone," Folmann wrote. "We’re also going to make AI tags on mod pages more prominent, displaying them immediately after adult-content tags so they’re easier to spot."

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that’s not going to happen," he continued. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules." New "permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods" are also being worked on, with the hopes of giving modders more control over how their works can be reused. Finally, Folmann noted that the site are "investing in security tooling and specialised staff" to address concerns over generative AI making "bespoke malicious code hidden inside mods" more prevalent.

Mod makers are being given a 60 day grace period to make sure their existing works meet the new rules, which'll run until January 2nd.

As you can imagine, the comments section of this Nexus Mods announcement is lively. Over on LinkedIn, Folmann patted himself on the back a bit about the mixed reception being an indicator the site are going about this the right way. "Some wanted a full ban. Some think we went too far. That tells me we drew the line where the real argument is," he declared, adding that "transparency beats prohibition". He also reiterated that his vision is of "modding that's Spotify-easy to play and GitHub-powerful to create, with humans in charge".

I reckon that with or without these changes, in the absence of its owners taking a strong stand browsing Nexus Mods is going to carry on be more of an exercise in ducking dodgy stuff than it was prior to most games' pages being splattered with the likes of icky AI-baked Geralt clones standing where decent screenshots of the actual game would've been more than adequate.

#4070. Monopoly Go x The Simpsons crossover is almost here

After a long wait and exhaustive leaks, the highly-anticipated Simpsons event will finally arrive in Monopoly Go very soon, alongside new content.

Monopoly Go players have been looking forward to a major crossover event for what felt like months, and though most of the details ended up leaking, nothing actually beats official information.

The world of The Simpsons has officially arrived in Monopoly Go, and there's a whole lot for players to dive into. The show's creative team even produced a new animated short, featuring Mr. Monopoly, and Mr. Burns.

Available June 3 through July 29, the new event allows Monopoly Go players to jump in the world of The Simpsons. You'll be able to build, and explore all around multiple iconic locations from the show.

Along the way, you'll run into Simpsons characters like Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and of course, Mr. Burns. Developer Scopely teamed up with the show's creative team to create many references, and Easter Eggs for you to discover. You'll find some of those on chance cards, but most of the world has been changed to be part of The Simpsons, including getting to bribe Chief Wiggum to escape jail.

The developer promises a deeply connected world with Simpsons narratives and characters that alter seasonal maps, and offer unique sticker sets and animated sequences to dive in. Incidentally, this is The Simpsons' first appearance in a mobile-exclusive game in 13 years.

Here's a breakdown of everything you can expect, straight from Scopely:

Episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

The Simpsons Run: Every two weeks, a new Springfield character will take over the Free Parking tile, kicking off character-driven runs.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

In fact, Capcom did remarkably well, scooping a total of six awards, including 'Studio of the Year'. The awards are mostly decided by public vote, with Requiem gaining 17% for its GOTY gong, ahead of Phantom Blade Zero at 16% and Crimson Desert at 15%.

Angela Sant'Albano, who played protagonist Grace Ashcroft in Requiem, won the award for 'Best Lead Performer', while the game also scooped up the 'Best Game Trailer' award for its short film starring Maika Monroe.

Requiem also won 'Console Game of the Year', while Onimusha: Way of the Sword won 'Best Audio Design'.

Unfortunately, no awards were handed out for first-party Nintendo games. Ocarina of Time, of course, launched too late to be eligible.

#4068. Two Major Developers Explain Why They Like And Dislike Making Games For Xbox Series S

"I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released (laughs)"

Over the years, we've heard all kinds of stories from all kinds of developers about whether they either like or dislike making games for the Xbox Series S, and former Tekken boss Katsuhiro Harada falls into the "dislike" category.

In a recent panel discussion that was transcribed by the folks at InvenGlobal, Harada noticed that a senior Xbox official was in the audience, and joked that he wanted to let them know how much he isn't a fan of the Xbox Series S.

"Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released (laughs)."

He then went on to explain that although the low memory is "an issue" of the Xbox Series S, the hardest part is that it's actually so similar to the Series X, but with "awkwardly lower performance". Harada also pointed out that players direct their complaints to the developers rather than Microsoft if they don't like the visuals and/or performance.

"Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance [...] Furthermore, in markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking "Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?"

Finally, he also noted that developing for the Nintendo Switch 2 is actually easier in some ways because it's a "distinct device for Nintendo fans", whereas the Xbox Series S is akin to "having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child" compared to putting in your "absolute best output" for the Xbox Series X.

Despite what it might seem like, a lot of this conversation seemed to be very lighthearted and full of laughs, and when Cyberpunk 2077's Paweł Sasko stepped in to highlight the benefits of the Xbox Series S including its affordable price and the ability to better optimise for low-spec platforms, Harada admitted that he made it sound a lot more attractive.

In fact, it was so convincing that Harada jokingly worried that it might lead to a similar Project Helix alternative!

Director Paweł: "Harada speaks a lot of truth. Players don't fully understand the technical context behind why fewer characters appear on screen or why visuals are downgraded. However, intensely optimizing for lower-spec platforms definitely brings the benefit of making the game run significantly better across all platforms—including PS5, high-end PCs, and handhelds like Steam Deck and ROG Ally.

And the biggest advantage of Series S is that its affordable price makes it accessible. Not every gamer can buy expensive high-end hardware, so from a developer's perspective, even if the strict constraints are painful, there is a silver lining in expanding market penetration to deliver the game to more players."

CEO Harada: "Director Paweł packaged Series S so gracefully that the Microsoft representative in the audience keeps nodding along. I'm worried they'll feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

It's best not to take any of this too seriously, but it does at least highlight the differing opinions throughout the industry about whether the Xbox Series S was a good or bad idea in hindsight.

From a consumer perspective at least, we reckon it was a fantastic idea. The Xbox Series S has continually managed to deliver incredible-looking games over the past six years, and in a time where console prices are constantly on the up, the Series S at least provides a somewhat affordable current-gen hardware option - at least if you find a good deal.

#4067. Trails beyond the Horizon Sequel Confirmed for 2027 as Falcom Steps Back from Remakes

The next game in Falcom's long running Trails series will be a sequel to Trails beyond the Horizon.

The developer confirmed this in its annual financial report, putting to rest mass speculation from fans of the franchise.

First released in 2024 in Japan, Trails beyond the Horizon features world-shifting story revelations and ends on one hell of a cliffhanger. Its sequel should, finally, have all of the answers — and it's set to launch before the end of September 2027.

The wait hasn't been quite so bad for western players, as Horizon was localised back in January of this year.

However, it should be noted that Falcom's report only refers to the sequel's Japanese release.

It'll be up to western publisher NIS America to work out whether a global launch is feasible, but I'd be shocked if it's not on the cards, because this is the first time in history that the west is actually fully caught up on the series.

Of course, this also means that Falcom is stepping back from its remakes for the time being. After the huge success of Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter and Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter, there was a suggestion that the studio would simply follow the money, and go straight into remaking Trails in the Sky the 3rd.

But it's no secret that the developer is ramping up towards the end of Trails as a whole — and so it's prioritising the next step in the franchise's current saga.

Falcom says that Horizon's sequel is the only major title it has in the works for 2027. As such, it's highly likely that its next remake will be targeting a 2028 release.

With all of this in mind, we should be getting our first look at Horizon's sequel in the coming months.

What are your hopes and dreams for the next Trails game? Go beyond the horizon in the comments section below.

#4066. Smash hit cyberpunk storekeeper Probably Stolen was originally a different, non-cyberpunk game that seemed destined to sink without trace

Publisher tinyBuild celebrates turnaround after very underwhelming demo numbers

Space station trading game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim has been doing rather well on Steam, attracting over 162,000 concurrent players last night. I've been feeling the urge to fire it up again myself, after my brief launch-day trawl through its quagmire of black market economics and factional rivalries.

The game's big numbers come as a shock given that it began life as another, non-cyberpunk kiosk job sim called Deepspace Emporium, which still has a Steam page as of writing. Deepspace Emporium seemed doomed to fizzle out in obscurity. But publisher tinyBuild got behind it regardless, working with developers Questing Goose to overhaul the art direction and lay on extra brainchips. The gamble paid off.

"Probably Stolen was initially a game under a different name with a released demo," summarises tinyBuild CEO Alex Nichiporchik on Twitter. "That demo peaked at 28 concurrent players. We loved the concept and gameplay, and worked with the dev to reinvent the visuals and focus on what works design wise. This is the result."

The original Deepspace Emporium seems very similar to Probably Stolen in broad strokes. The core of the game is haggling with strung-out ne'er-do-wells, buying or selling goods of varying quality and legality in order to surf a fluctuating market and pay the rent. It's Papers, Please, but you're searching for fake watermarks on cigarette packets, and wondering whether you dare stock contraband weaponry. You also have to appease or outmanouevre factions with competing interests, from station security to underworld barons.

From what I've played, Probably Stolen essentially takes all that and pumps up the Netrunner parallels with posher visuals. Not having played the now-unavailable Deepspace demo, I can't say how much intrigue it adds to all the shady transactions going on beneath the hood.

I'm not blown away by Probably Stolen's pixelart – I find it quite flavourless, as depictions of cyberpunk space stations go – but it has pleasing texture. I am disproportionately fond of the rolled-up sleeping mat beneath my counter. Looks nicely padded! Still, the meat of this game is undoubtedly the vast collection of items you can get your greasy fingers on, with a choice of retail lines and vocational pathways such as gunsmith and chemist. You can sell rat corpses, tins of caviar, robotic hands, scavenged shotguns, and purple tubers of uncertain origin. I am Commander Silverhand, and this is my favourite store on the Citadel.

It's lovely to think of a developer transforming a probable write-off into a chart-topper by means of some canny plumping and reorganising. The situation is almost certainly more complicated than Nichiporchik makes it sound. Still, let's take the opportunity to reminisce moist-eyed about a few other games that underwent a dramatic visual transformation during development.

The obvious one is Team Fortress 2, which once upon a time looked like a prototype Silent Hill environment with some khaki toy soldiers. Gearbox worked similar sorcery upon Borderlands, which once looked like a hungover Fallout 3. The prevailing wisdom is that piping in some colour and whimsy propelled these games to greatness, but who knows, perhaps if they'd clung to the old "football stadium toilet bowl" vibe, they'd have made an extra billion apiece. Any other precedents come to your mind?

#4064. Romancing SaGa 3: Destinies United Will Launch Earlier Than Expected On Switch 2

Square Enix popped up at the September Nintendo Direct to reveal Romancing SaGa 3: Destinies United for Switch and Switch 2. It came with a 16th February 2027 release date, but the studio has changed its plans in the months since, and we're now getting our hands on it a few weeks earlier.

According to Square Enix, the HD remake will now launch on 4th February 2027, with pre-orders going live on the eShop next week on 19th November.

For those who missed the initial announcement, this remake gives the 1995 RPG a modern facelift, complete with brand-new visuals, fully voice-acted scenes, new arrangements of Kenji Ito's iconic score, and a few other tweaks previously deployed in Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven.

Most importantly, this new version has made some changes to the original's Free-Form Scenario system with the goal of making the main story and its eight (yes, eight) protagonists easier to follow.

Alongside the standard edition, Square Enix is also releasing a Digital Deluxe Edition for the game, which bundles in bonus costumes and equipment, a battle music toggle, and additional items for the Business and War Mode minigames. You'll even get to start the game 72 hours earlier than everyone else. Nice.

#4063. Xbox Brings Its Free Tier Of Cloud Gaming To Loads More Players Today

You may recall that back in July, Xbox announced a new free version of Xbox Cloud Gaming that would allow you to play games at no charge, but you'd be forced to deal with ads as a compromise.

That tier of Xbox Cloud Gaming was in testing for months, but as of today (November 11th), it's rolled out publicly - meaning the vast majority of Xbox users around the world should now have access to it.

Xbox has been very quiet about it today so far, but based on what we've seen around the web, the free tier of Xbox Cloud Gaming will provide you with a 30-minute slot to stream "select games from your library" as well as select free-to-play games, after which time you'll be kicked off and will have to start a new session.

You'll see ads before the session begins, and seemingly never again throughout your 30-minute playtime.

"You can stream select games for free by watching ads before each gaming session. Session time limits apply. After a session ends, you can watch another set of ads to start a new session."

News Xbox Introduces Free Game Streaming With Ads, Outlines Five Principles They'll Adhere To

Rolling out now as a "test" for Xbox Insiders

Despite the rapid session length, this could prove a popular option for anyone who wants to play GTA 6 on Xbox One (for example) without being forced to pay anything for Xbox Cloud Gaming. We'd urge some caution for now though, as Xbox has yet to confirm whether GTA 6 will be one of the "select" games that supports this feature.

Meanwhile, the cloud playtime limits that were announced a while ago for Xbox Game Pass members have now started kicking in, which also means you can now purchase "Cloud Playtime" to top it up if you run out.

The prices for this here in the UK are as follows:

Curiously though, I've checked the new "Cloud Playtime" option in the Settings menu on my Xbox Series X and I'm being informed that I've still got "Unlimited" access to Xbox Cloud Gaming with my Ultimate membership, so it might be worth checking the same thing on your end and seeing what it says for you.

I'm not the only person who's spotted something similar:

Anyway, we've thrown Xbox's official tweet up above, and you can hit the link in it to find out even more details.

#4062. Try Hellraiser: Revival in This New PS5 Demo, Out Now

Saber Interactive is letting you sample the opening moments of Hellraiser: Revival via a new PS5 demo that's been put on the PS Store today. This isn't one that's tied to PS Plus Premium; it's a free download for everyone.

You'll get to play through the game's prologue, and then a "portion" of the first chapter. This means you'll get to see a lot of what the title is all about: gore, action, sex... and more gore. The first hour or so lets you enter the Labyrinth, and then chapter one is more of a stealth sequence where you have to escape your captors.

Since the demo breaks up a piece of the full game, I don't believe that your progress would carry over if you were to buy it afterwards. Still, it's a nice sample of a horror game I had a lot of fun with a few weeks ago.

Opinion Hey, That Hellraiser: Revival Game Is Pretty Good

If you like what you play, Hellraiser: Revival is full price at the moment: £34.99 / $39.99 on the PS Store. I expect the game will go on sale at some point before the year is out, though, so it might be worth waiting and keeping an eye on our coverage of the PS Store sales to come.

It seems that Ruaridh Mollica is hopeful for a Young Avengers movie

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ruaridh Mollica is absolutely down for a Young Avengers movie... especially after the big reveal in the final episode of VisionQuest.

Warning: there are massive spoilers for VisionQuest episode 8 ahead!

In the season finale of VisionQuest, Tommy finally reunites with his brother Billy – and it all becomes a very sweet family reunion. After Vision saves the world from a vengeful Ultron (again), Billy appears and is pulled in for a rather heartwarming group hug.

"Do the words 'young' and 'Avengers' mean anything to you?" Iman Vellani asked Mollica during a special VisionQuest episode of the Marvel podcast she hosts with Frank Alvarez.

"They mean a dream I would love to come true," he replied.

Now that Tommy aka Speed has arrived, and has finally teamed up with Billy aka Wiccan, this means the following comic book-accurate Young Avengers members are currently in the MCU: Speed, Wiccan, Kamala Khan aka Ms. Marvel, Kate Bishop, Cassie Lang, Skaar, Lisa Molinari, and America Chavez. I think those are enough characters for a standalone movie, wouldn't you say?

There is also the fact that the extra post-credits scene at the end of VisionQuest implies that Tommy and Billy could be in Avengers: Doomsday, as the scene sees Wanda resurrected by Doom... but seemingly put under his spell. There's a Young Avengers comic book arc where Wanda goes missing, loses her memory, and becomes Doom's bride. But we'll just have to see on December 18.

VisionQuest is streaming now in its entirety on Disney Plus. For even more, check out our VisionQuest review or our VisionQuest ending explained.

#4060. "Keep talking about it": Raw Power Games call for Wishlist aid as they, and their historical strategy sandbox Chronicles: Medieval, lose funding

Raw Power Games, an independent studio comprising veteran developers of The Witcher 3, Total War: Three Kingdoms, and Crusader Kings III (among others), have called on players for support after losing their funding - an existential threat to both the organisation and to their debut, the still-in-development historical strategy game Chronicles: Medieval.

In a statement posted last week, Raw Power announced that "the necessary funding" behind the studio was no longer in place, despite Chronicles: Medieval – which was unveiled last year with an expensive-looking, Tom Hardy-narrated trailer – apparently being within touching distance of its planned early access launch. Hardy or no Hardy, however, the statement declared that they aren't "going down without a fight", hinting at talks with what could be possible new investors, asking interested would-be fans to "keep talking about" the game, and encouraging its inclusion on Steam Wishlists.

A few days on, the impact of this rallying call remains unclear. Raw Power Games have made no further statements, and Chronicles: Medieval does not seem to appear on Steam's own list of Top Wishlisted games. SteamDB have it at #26 in their desire-o-rankings, representing no change from its position immediately before the funding announcement was made, and while the game's Steam follower count has increased by over 1,000 week-on-week – significantly more so than surrounding games in the list – that doesn't feel like the kind of wild grassroots support that might save a dozens-strong studio.

Still, as my childhood television used to say, every little helps, and I'm inclined to hope for Raw Power's survival if only as an antidote to the enthusiasm-poisining dread of seeing so many other developers being laid off and shut down. Chronicles: Medieval looks promisingly ambitious too, mashing up sprawling Mount & Blade-style battles with an RPG-flavoured strategy layer that involves the player's custom-created character ascending the snooty social hierarchy of 14th century England. Best of luck to everyone trying to get it over the early access line.

#4059. Review: Harold Halibut (Switch 2) - A Creative Marvel That Suffers In The Back Half

This won’t be the first Harold Halibut review to mention being wowed by one of the game’s pre-launch trailers during its release on other platforms back in 2024. Back then, the game’s stop-motion aesthetic — with character models based on scans of real marionettes, and its tactile hand-wrought sets — looked like nothing I’d ever seen.

Coupled with the atmospheric music and the promise of engaging characters and ambitious emotional storytelling, it became, in my eyes, an absolute must-play. And of course it did – its story of a crashed spaceship and its crew, stranded on an ocean planet, looked like a Wes Anderson animation, like Isle of Dogs or Fantastic Mr Fox. In terms of defining what games are capable of, I was ready for Harold Halibut to set new standards. I was convinced it would be a sure-fire 10/10.

Now as I write this review, I wonder if part of the stunned feeling was just a little confusion about how such an ambitious storytelling production would translate into a game. And it’s a fair question – after finishing Harold Halibut and watching that trailer again, I notice very little gameplay. A little walking around perhaps, but not much else.

2024’s reviews were, indeed, mixed. The development team, Slow Bros, an independent game studio based in Cologne, had certainly left an impression. Some reviewers declared Harold Halibut a breath of fresh air and a work of art, while others clearly hit a wall when it came to a lack of gameplay. For me, at different times, I found myself in either camp.

My notes from the opening few hours are as excited as I’ve ever written. The pleasant world and characters set out their stall early. Harold Halibut is an enjoyable presence, a handyman surrounded as he goes about his days by a variety of memorable characters.

I enjoyed the atmosphere, the story, and how Harold’s Ship, the Fedora 1, is run by a quirky corporation called All Water, who themselves are balancing the commercial benefits of their transportation system with a lack of resources. Despite the risk for on-the-nose satire, nothing ever felt heavy-handed. At all times ‘character’ came first, to the game’s great benefit.

I controlled Harold as he went about his janitorial tasks — cleaning filters, clearing rooms of boxes, fixing machinery — and liked the enjoyable if simple gameplay loop of exploring the ship, the social areas, the science areas, and having the freedom to choose where to go and who to chat to. These moments — controlling Harold’s marionette, seeing all the lovely sets, and discovering layers and depth in the characters, helped by impressive voice acting — fulfilled the initial promise I’d seen in that trailer.

Harold Halibut was over 10 years in the making, and took less than 10 seconds to fall in love with. As a whole, it’s a beautiful work of art, a thought-provoking story with excellent character development. However, it’s best played docked due to performance issues (primarily frame rate) whilst in handheld. Regardless, still worth a play.

I was effectively playing an animation, and it was wonderful. For the best part of five hours, I was never bored, and in fact often delighted as little variations in the gameplay kept things fresh, as characters bonded, and as the plot became alive with subplots and the promise of a grand finale I just had to see.

But then, as my playtime extended, a few elements brought me back down to earth.

First, I sensed some bloat creep into the gameplay, and I started to feel a little less happy about the repetitiveness of running about delivering messages and catching up with the crew. Second, there was a subtle slowdown in the overall pace of the story. And third, the narrative clearly started taking over the gameplay a little too much. There were long periods where I either didn’t even need to press a button, or otherwise do little more than walk around to trigger the next cutscene.

Harold Halibut is, of course, a narrative-focused adventure. I’ve enjoyed games like Night in the Woods and Oxenfree, but for me the 11-hour runtime for the main storyline here could have done with a trim in the second half.

It’s not that the cutscenes were a problem, but coming back to short snippets of gameplay after long breaks only to be tasked with running back and forth multiple times between, say, two locations (which happened once) felt a bit like hard work.

Just when I wanted the storytelling momentum to build, Harold Halibut lost a little of its focus. The themes and creativity established during the early interactions with the cast — the delightful running-enthusiast postman, the shopkeeper trying to adjust his work-life balance, and Harold’s ex Sunny, struggling to define her life goals — faded into the background as Harold’s storyline took over.

I loved Harold, but except for one soliloquy, he had, for much of the game, seemed more of a fun, pleasant vessel for meeting the other citizens of the spaceship. This isn’t a big complaint, but it contributed to a sense of the second half leaving behind some of the things that made the opening so great.

The last thing to say is that the Switch 2 port isn’t quite as pretty as other incarnations, while still being playable and enjoyable. The camera stutters during zooms and pans, which are frequent thanks to the game’s cinematic style.

It’s a shame because the visuals are clearly one of Harold Halibut’s big strengths, but, ultimately, this is still a very playable port. I can’t say these issues impacted my enjoyment at all.

Back in 2024, I imagined writing a review for Harold Halibut and rounding up the final score to a 10. I like Harold Halibut a lot. I enjoyed the story, the heart, the characters — and of course I loved the visuals — but I also felt the balance of gameplay, narrative, and pacing wasn’t quite there for me, and that this had an overall impact on how well it works as a game.

Now looking back at those reviews from the original release — the spread of besotted 10s to the more cautious 6s — I think they all have a point. Harold Halibut is a creative marvel. It is a work of art and it’s worth playing to appreciate all that wonderful craft. But the pace can also drag and sometimes gameplay takes a little too much of a back seat. Ultimately, it’s a curiosity with a lot of heart. It struggles to balance its elements, but I’m very happy to have played it. If the visuals and storytelling style appeal, then it’s definitely worth a look.

Review copy provided by Slow BrosHow we review productsScoring Policy

#4058. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

Now over 100 hours in, catch up on the events of the first two parts of the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is the third and final instalment of the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy that reimagines the 1997 PS1 JRPG classic while incorporating the wider universe known as The Compilation of Final Fantasy 7 (which includes spin-offs like PSP's Crisis Core: Final Fantasy 7, and even movies like Advent Children).

While there's still time to catch up on the first two parts ahead of Final Fantasy 7 Revelation's impending April 8, 2027 release, which will conclude the saga, you've come to the right place if you're after a condensed catch up on the story so far of Cloud Strife and co's fight to save the planet, and how this retelling also deviates from the original game. It goes without saying that there will be spoilers ahead. If you're in need of a refresher without making time for hundreds of hours re-adventuring, or just want to catch the climax of Cloud and Sephiroth's ultimate clash, then we've got you covered.

If you're ready to make like a chocobo, then let's go!

With the remake trilogy drawing to a close early 2027, we get ready for the epic conclusion with our Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Big Preview across hands-on impressions, dev access, and deep dives into the whole adventure so far.

We kick off with Final Fantasy 7 Remake, which covers just the original game's opening section in Midgar, a multi-tiered dystopian metropolis controlled by fascist megacorporation Shinra. Just like the original Final Fantasy 7, it opens with protagonist Cloud, a former member of SOLDIER, Shinra's elite military, who's now working as a mercenary for eco-terrorist group Avalanche. Their mission is to blow up Mako Reactor 1 in order to disrupt Shinra's activities of harvesting Mako energy, which they believe is sucking the planet's life force dry.

With the bombing mission a success – though the remake deviates from the original by making Avalanche's bomb a dud while President Shinra actually sets off the real explosion that's far deadlier than intended – the group's leader Barret Wallace feels emboldened to target Mako Reactor 5, with Cloud also joining the mission, alongside his childhood friend Tifa Lockhart from the Sector 7 undercity's slums.

Between these missions, we also see how else Final Fantasy 7 Remake expands and deviates from the original game, as we learn of Avalanche member Jessie' backstory as a theater actress who leaves behind her stage career after her father falls into a coma due to Mako poisoning, while Cloud has visions of the game's true threat, Sephiroth, and a chance encounter with flower girl Aerith Gainsborough is interrupted by the presence of mysterious hooded specters.

However, the Mako Reactor 5 mission goes awry, leading to Cloud being separated from Avalanche and crashing into a church in the Sector 5 slums where he once again encounters Aerith, who is being pursued by Shinra's covert ops Turks unit. Aerith joins Cloud on his way back to Sector 7 when they notice a carriage passing by, which Tifa is inside, heading to the manor of Don Corneo, a slumlord in Sector 5, home to the seedy entertainment district of Wall Market.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

After an elaborate makeover for both Cloud and Aerith to infiltrate Don Corneo's manor to rescue Tifa, they learn from the Don that Shinra plans to drop the Sector 7 plate onto the slums below to destroy Avalanche, regardless of all the innocent people who would also be killed. Despite their best efforts, the plate drops, causing huge destruction and casualties, including the death of Avalanche members Biggs and Jessie, while Aerith allows herself to be captured by Shinra in exchange for the safety of Marlene, Barret's daughter.

Resolved to rescue Aerith, Cloud, Barrett, and Tifa infiltrate Shinra's headquarters before its head scientist Hojo can experiment on her. Aerith is revealed to be the last descendant of the Cetra (also known as the Ancients), a mystical precursor race connected to the Lifestream, which Shinra wants to exploit in order to gain access to the Mako-rich 'Promised Land'.

During Aerith's rescue and the group's escape, they are joined by Red XIII, a dog-like creature who has also been a captive of Hojo's experiments, while President Shinra is killed by Sephiroth, only to be quickly succeeded by his son Rufus.

As Cloud leads the team with a motorcycle to escape the rest of Shinra's forces and reach Midgar's outskirts, it culminates in a confrontation with Sephiroth and the hooded specters that Red XIII calls Whispers. Their presence throughout the story have been to essentially act as arbiters of fate, which in a meta twist, ensures that events play out just like they did in the original story of Final Fantasy 7. This explains their intervention in moments where fate almost diverges, such as ensuring that Cloud spares Turk member Reno during their fight, that he doesn't leave Avalanche high and dry on the fifth Mako reactor mission, or that Barret survives what should have been a fatal stabbing from Sephiroth.

In a battle against the whispers and Sephiroth, the team successfully defy fate, and as they leave Midgar, we see implications of how the universe has split into into alternate timelines, with one where Biggs and Jessie survived the falling of the Sector 7 plate, and another where another SOLDIER named Zack – someone Aerith had been previously in love with – survives an attack by Shinra forces and is seen carrying a wounded Cloud to Midgar (he famously dies in both the original's flashback scenes, and PSP sequel Crisis Core).

While much of FF7 Remake kept us guessing as to how close events would hew to the original game, and what role the Whispers functioned, this striking ending blows the doors wide open – leaving many to wonder if the sequel would have much in common with the original events at all.

Alongside the events of Final Fantasy 7 Remake, Intermission follows Yuffie, a young ninja who has come to Midgar on a mission from the interim Wutai government – Shinra's arch rival – to steal Shinra's 'Ultimate Materia' with the help of her partner Sonon and a local Avalanche cell, where it also emerges that Barret's Avalanche is considered a more radical fringe breakaway faction from a broader Avalanche organization.

Yuffie and Sonon infiltrate a lab underneath Shinra HQ where they battle against Scarlet, Shinra's head of weapon research, as well as top-secret military organization Deepground, including one of their leaders Nero the Sable. While the mission ends in failure as there turns out to be no 'Ultimate Materia', and Sonon sacrifices himself to ensure Yuffie's escape, this ordeal gives the young Wutai ninja the resolve to find likeminded allies to help her bring down Shinra.

Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth begins by exploring more of the first entry's alternate timeline split through Zack, where the Avalanche members are seen wounded and taken captive while Aerith is comatose. Zack manages to take both her and Cloud to hide out at her mother Elmyra's house. It's gradually revealed that in this timeline, the planet's Mako has already been fully depleted as people brace for the imminent end of the world.

Back in Remake's original timeline, Cloud and the party have left behind Midgar and arrive in the town of Kalm where he relays his past with Sephiroth when both were assigned to investigate a Mako reactor in Cloud's hometown of Nibelheim five years ago. During this mission, Sephiroth suffered a mental breakdown after learning that he was artificially created from the cells of an extra-terrestrial life-form called Jenova, his identity crisis resulting in the massacre and destruction of Nibelheim before returning to the reactor to recover the body of his 'mother'.

The party decides to pursue Sephiroth by following the trail of 'black robes', former Shinra test subjects, who Cloud believes will lead them to Sephiroth. They journey across the wider world, including the Shinra-controlled port city of Junon during an inauguration parade for Shinra's new president Rufus; the sun-kissed Costa Del Sol where Aerith and Tifa want to let their hair down but Hojo is also using the black robes as part of his heinous experiments; Barret's hometown of Mt. Corel where the group learns he is blamed for the explosion of its Mako reactor; the Gold Saucer filled with minigames and home to the popular play Loveless; Zack's hometown of Gongaga; Red XIII's hometown of Cosmo Canyon, where it's revealed his real name is Nanaki and despite his deep voice, his age is developmentally equivalent to a 15 or 16 year-old human; there's even a return to Nibelheim, which Shinra has eerily rebuilt in its entirety.

Along the way, new members also join the party, including Wutai ninja Yuffie, remote-controlled robot cat Cait Sith, pilot Cid Highwind who owns the dual-propeller airplane the Tiny Bronco, and the vampiric beast-transforming ex-Turk Vincent Valentine (the latter two are non-playable in Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth). They also encounter several appearances of Weapons, gigantic guardians that act as part of the Planet's self-defense. Despite defeating the Arbiter of Fate, the whispers also return but in new variants, with white whispers allying themselves with the Planet, while the black ones are aiding Sephiroth's plans. The party soon learns that his ultimate plan is to use the Black Materia to summon Meteor to destroy the Planet.

This culminates in a race between Cloud's party and Shinra through the Temple of the Ancients in search of the Black Materia, all while Wutai openly declares war on Shinra. Despite the party's successful efforts in securing the Black Materia, Sephiroth takes control of Cloud's mind, forcing him to hand it over, and explains his plans of 'Reunion', which would forcibly fuse the alternate universes together into a paradise he can rule over.

In the ensuing chaos, Aerith goes it alone to try and stop Sephiroth, and the party traces her to the Forgotten Capital, an ancient Cetran City. They are blocked by a horde of whispers from entering the temple where Aerith is, but a tear opens enough for Cloud to go through, where he finds Aerith attempting to pray for help from the Planet to stop Sephiroth.

Whereas in the original story, Sephiroth tries to force Cloud to kill her, this time the whispers try to manipulate Cloud to use his Buster Sword, though he resists. Sephiroth descends from the sky to get the job done himself, and while Cloud blocks and disarms him, a distortion in the timeline makes it so that Sephiroth does kill Aerith, sending her White Materia into the water. While this causes the whispers to disperse, allowing the rest of the party to catch and fight Jenova like in the original game, Cloud is separated and finds his timeline converging with Zack's.

Zack's timeline, meanwhile, has been fracturing into multiple threads, each based on a different decision he makes, including trying to save a version of Biggs who survived Remake's destruction of Sector 7. Ultimately, Zack also comes face to face with Sephiroth, temporarily having Cloud assist as they fight their common foe across universes, while Aerith from an alternate timeline comes to Cloud's aid in the final battle. Although the fight forces Sephiroth to retreat, in the current timeline, the party members mourn Aerith's death, even though Cloud still seems to be able to see her.

As the party lick their wounds and continue pursuing Sephiroth on Cid's Tiny Bronco, Cloud discovers he still has the Black Materia, which he fuses into the Buster Sword, while he is also able to see a black rift in the sky that the others cannot. As he says goodbye to Aerith's ghost, who stays behind, Cloud vows to stop Sephiroth. This time, it's not just about stopping him from destroying the Planet and controlling the Lifestream like it was in the PS1 game, but from controlling all realities and timelines in the many universes of Final Fantasy 7.

What will happen next in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation remains to be seen, especially when it comes to how closely it'll stay to the final arc of the PS1 game. If you're curious to know more, join me later in the week as I unravel 8 story threads I hope Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will resolve, and continue exploring this epic saga's narrative.

Fancy more fantasy? Check out our best RPGs and best JRPGs rankings for more adventures worth unsheathing your Buster Sword to tackle.

#4055. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#4054. Cosy Train Sim 'Station To Station' Arrives On Switch 2 Later This Month

Do you like trains? Of course you do, who doesn't like trains. Stupid question. Anyway, you're in luck, dear reader. The cosy train sim Station to Station is making its way to the Switch 2, launching on 26th November 2026.

Boasting lovely voxel visuals, Station to Station starts you off with a handful of rural structures, tasking you with creating stations and connections to expand your world and transform it into a lush, thriving landscape.

While it's ultimately a relaxing experience, you can also earn high scores by engaging with more strategic gameplay, allowing you to stack bonuses and multiply your income.

On Switch 2, you can expect to find mouse controls along with the game's Creative Mode, letting you explore community designs and share your own. The main game will contain 54 levels set across 7 regions.

Over on Steam, Station to Station currently commands a total of 1,248 user reviews, of which 89% are positive. It's also earned solid scores from critics too, including 8/10 from IGN and 4/5 from Tech Radar.

Mini Review Locomoto (Switch) - On The Right Cosy Track, But Has A Few Train Faults

Do you think you'll pick up Station to Station when it launches later this month? Let us know with a comment in the usual place.
