#4000. 'There Is No Truth to These Claims': Marvel 1943 Not Cancelled, But Doesn't Sound Great

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra – the highly promising superhero game starring Captain America and Black Panther – has not been cancelled, despite rumours to the contrary earlier today.

A fan account claimed on X (or Twitter) that the project, fronted by former Uncharted lead Amy Hennig, had been scrapped. That post has since been deleted.

But Kotaku gained access to a message posted in dev Skydance Games’ private Slack channel, where executive producer Lu Gigliotti confirmed with leadership that the reports aren’t true.

The game – first announced in 2019 – was originally due out earlier this year, but has now been pushed back to 2027.

And based on further reporting from Kotaku, you may not want to get your hopes up too high for this one.

While the project is purportedly progressing and is poised to hit an “alpha” milestone soon, it’s allegedly over budget and has been scaled back significantly.

Curiously, journalist Rebekah Valentine reports that the title was originally intended for Netflix, but transitioned to consoles like PS5 during development.

As such, gameplay is said to be light, “primarily using only one button and lacking significant interaction”.

If you felt this year’s Marvel’s Wolverine was a bit basic, then it sounds like this may end up even more simplistic by comparison.

#3999. Remedy revenue soars by 226% following release of Control Resonant, the developer's fastest-selling game ever

Remedy - the developer behind the recently released Control Resonant - has released a scorcher of a quarterly financial report. It shows that following Resonant's release in September, the company's revenue surged by 226 percent, bringing in €39.6m in Q3.

This performance was described as "a defining milestone for the company" by CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon. The company reported a €0.6m operating profit this quarter, a fair leap upwards from the €16.4m loss from this time last year.

There are some interesting highlights to this sudden surging performance. For one, the US made up nearly half of Control Resonant's players across PC and console, followed by Chinese-speaking regions and then the UK.

Perhaps most crucially is that nearly half of Control Resonant's players were entirely new to the franchise, with the company stating: "Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy."

Control (2019) also saw a bump up in sales thanks to the release of Control Resonant, showing a stronger performance this quarter than the past two quarters this year as well as its comparison period (this quarter last year).

Remedy's CEO now believes the focus for the studio is to "get Resonant into the hands of more players." He continues to say the game has provided a solid foundation for growth as other projects (including the Max Payne 1 & 2 remake) are in the works. In short, things appear to be looking rather good for Remedy.

Control Resonant was an artistically impressive but critically divisive game. While many praised the series' adventure into third person action, some felt it had less of a narrative bite than its predecessor. Nonetheless the game quickly blasted past one million sales after launch.

Control loreheads shouldn't put too much stock into what The Board says in Control Resonant - the devs say it's "basically gibberish"

#3998. Airframe Ultra's PS1 cyberpunk city is an amazing tribute to G-Police and WipEout, and I wish you people would slow down to appreciate it

But what if we could gawk at the dumpsters

I do not wish to "rule the streets" of Megacity West, dear creators of Airframe Ultra. I wish to be ravished by them, rubbing my face against the rusty corrugated metal of the shipping containers, and savouring the acid blue waters of the bay. I do not want to "become the one thing with freedom in a city of billions: A racer." I want to become the other thing with freedom in a city of billions: a person who slowly drives or – whisper it - walks around just looking at stuff, because gadzooks, this is one of the prettiest PS1 cyberpunk burgs I've laid eyes on.

Those eroded pastel chevrons. Those seductively wobbling vertices. That electric reef of a downtown backdrop, murderously luring your gaze from the on-coming trucks. That layer of invigorating crackle over everything. Every moment or so, I dismount from my hoverbike to inspect some concrete ruin I could swear I last saw in G-Police, or ponder the resemblance between a subway tunnel and WipEout 2097's Gare d'Europa. Then, somebody waps me in the skull with a stop sign at 300 kilometres an hour. But I was already stopped, frantic stranger! Your brutal poetic ironies are wasted on me.

Despite my best efforts, Airframe Ultra is a battle racer. It's co-developed by Videocult, the people behind Rain World – a game it looks nothing like, but is comparable to in the sense that there is an ocean of industrial refuse to navigate, and you will very often die. Each battle race is broken into sprints around a branching course that has been smashed together by the forces of urban decay. You will corkscrew down storm drains and barge through old abandoned clifftop mansions under a scarlet sun, zip along deadly flyovers and thread the barely legible layouts of high density slums.

Your hoverbike handles like a bronco full of helium, and that's before you start wanging it off the gloriously marbled, low-poly rubbish heaps that stud the city, shunting the game's camera through surfaces and exposing the map's underside in what the absolute squares amongst my readers will doubtless deem "an inelegance", but which true turbojunkeys will appreciate for its makeshift exuberance.

You've got a boost button which generally gets you exploded – and all that's before you get to the time-limited battle arenas that bookend each sprint. Here, players attempt to slaughter each other as much as possible, spending collectible cash on floating weapon pick-ups that range from bent pipes to Gatling guns and EMP grenades. Then it's off for another sprint. The first player to earn 10 points and place first in a subsequent sprint wins the match. I have not won many matches. My primary goal right now in Airframe Ultra is persuading everybody to stop and swap some emotes, while I coo over an amazing piece of graffiti I've found.

My efforts to make Airframe Ultra a walking sim aren't just about scenery. The game is surprisingly engrossing on foot, with some woozy tank controls that make me think of the experimental days before every third-person control scheme became a variation on Assassin's Creed, Uncharted or Gears of War. You have to hammer a button to run, for instance, and you'll wind yourself fast. You can also perform punches and kicks in four directions, with grander attacks to discover by smooshing together inputs. You'd best believe I burst into tears when I realised what this reminded me of: it's Bungie's Oni! The game with the finest martial arts system ever coded! There are more obvious influences, like Road Rash, but in these grim days of endless parrying, I'll take all the Konoko callbacks I can get.

Ahhhhh. But if only this had a proper single player mode. Online and local splitscreen with drop-in bot support are all you get. I wouldn't say Airframe is the most balanced deathracer, either. In my experience, and do bear in mind I mostly try to avoid the racing component, victory typically goes to whoever lands a fat cash reserve and grabs an AK47. That mild shambolicness is arguably part of the charm, in that it supplies incentive to stop and drink in the atmosphere. These streets are big and broken and beautiful enough for all of us, friends. Let us rule them together. Read more on Steam.

#3997. Acer Predator Atlas 8 (G3 Extreme) review

The fact this is the cheapest way of getting Intel's G3 is both a boon for Acer and an indictment of the memory crisis. If you've gotta buy soon, this offers perhaps the best price-to-performance ratio above $1,000.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Intel's G3 Extreme is a mighty impressive chip, and easily the headline feature of Acer's Predator Atlas 8. If you're looking to get the best handheld Panther Lake chip right now, Acer has swooped in at pretty much the cheapest price point on the market.

And if that's all you want, the Atlas 8 has my blessing. It's a solid device that makes use of the chip and offers compromises in memory and storage capacity (in the American market) to bring that cost down. Not only that, but if you buy one right now, you get a heaping of goodies with it.

But if you don't need top-of-the-line specs to have a good time, the Atlas 8 instead becomes just one of many very, very solid, yet very, very expensive handhelds on offer in a time that has become worse and worse thanks to the memory crisis.

✅ You want the G3 Extreme but cheaper: The Atlas 8 undercuts both MSI and OneXPlayer in pricing for a G3 Extreme handheld.

❌ You play fighters or platformers primarily: The D-pad is mushy and lacks distinction, making it unsatisfying and a tad unruly.

The fact this is the cheapest way of getting Intel's G3 is both a boon for Acer and an indictment of the memory crisis. If you've gotta buy soon, this offers perhaps the best price-to-performance ratio above $1,000.

8-inch WUXGA 1920 x 1200 (120 Hz refresh rate and 500 nits peak brightness)

The memory capacity is around average (Though lower than the high-end G3 Extreme offerings from MSI and OneXPlayer), and the storage is below average for a high-end handheld if you buy it in America.

Though 512 GB of storage isn't awful in a device you only want for gaming, the G3 Extreme is strong enough to take on even beefy, big-budget games, so it's a shame that the Atlas 8 can't hold all that many at once.

You are getting a strong feature set even outside of that chip, though. For one, TMR Sticks make for not only more efficient battery usage, but snappy, responsive controls. And you get Hall effect triggers too.

In a handful of games, with upscaling on and off (35 W plugged in)

Performance is the name of the game for the Acer Predator Atlas 8, and boy, does it perform. Compared to the Z2 Extreme, I saw figures generally between 30% and 50% better, but it manages to double the fps in Metro Exodus.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

That performance bump is especially noticeable in games like Black Myth: Wukong, which are just below what I'd consider playable on Z2 Extreme and just about playable on the G3 Extreme. The G3 Extreme is the best gaming handheld chip right now, and the Atlas 8 getting less capacious memory than the MSI Claw 8 Ex AI+ CG3EM does not hold it back much in my testing. In fact, in some places, it even performs ever so slightly better.

Scores in major productivity suites and benchmarking tools (35 W plugged in)

At 860 grams, the Atlas 8 is a bit on the heavy side. It's balanced well, not feeling particularly heavy on either side, but you do notice that weight after long gaming sessions. I'm fond of the textured grips, but I do feel spoiled by the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 I used prior, thanks to its great feel and small cutaway between the screen and the grips.

However, I would simply pick a different handheld if you are planning on playing a heavy amount of fighting games or platformers, as the D-Pad is mushy, making it not only lacking in accuracy but generally unsatisfying to use. It's hard to make out when you actually hit buttons on the D-Pad, and it has very little distinction between different directions, making corner hits quite awkward. In Animal Well, I swapped to the thumbstick and never looked back.

The triggers and bumpers are solid, though, and the macro buttons on the back are satisfying to hit. You can even use a toggle just under the triggers to swap them from micro switches to full travel. That's an on-the-fly level of customisation that's admirable at best, and unnoticeable at worst.

Everything else about the Acer Predator Atlas 8 feels high quality in terms of feel. It's sturdy, with buttons placed well, and they're satisfyingly clacky without being too loud. The sound on the triggers is too hollow for my liking, but they feel smooth to the touch and are plenty responsive.

Speaking of loud, the speakers built into the Atlas 8 can really thump. They are in the bottom left and bottom right of the device, near the screen, making them quite immersive in use. They're not the highest quality, with the clashing of steel sounding more tinny than I'd usually ask for, but they're certainly not bad given their size.

With fans set to auto and performance mode at the 35 W Turbo mode, the fans are noticeable (once again, I have been spoiled by the X20), especially in intensive games like Phantom Blade Zero. But they're not so loud that they would put me off using this handheld in its high-wattage mode. I measured the fans to be around 40 decibels at their peak (around a whisper), with it averaging 28-35 decibels in intensive games. Whilst benchmarking, that went up to the 50-decibel mark, though only very briefly.

Acer says it has equipped the Atlas 8 with a custom Predator AeroBlade cooling, and in practice, it's certainly cooler than the likes of the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X and Lenovo Legion G S (though it doesn't beat the X20).

It certainly gets fairly hot internally, but with the fans pointing upwards, I never noticed any of that heat on my fingertips.

Recorded in HW Info whilst performing gaming benchmarks (35 W plugged in)

Windows on a handheld can still be awkward. The Atlas 8 comes built in with Xbox's handheld software, which is somewhat like Microsoft's attempt at Steam, but it's not totally smooth sailing in any direction (though it's more efficient than Windows). For instance, you can't get Intel drivers through the Acer Predator software built into the device as you might expect, so you still have to go through the Intel updater or search the internet, except with a touchscreen. And the Xbox mode still opens up Steam independently if you want to play a Steam game.

As well as this, the Atlas 8 has two dedicated buttons to open up Acer's software, the Acer Predator Sense, but it doesn't always work on the first try, and I haven't figured out exactly why this is yet. The button on the left-hand side opens up a quick bar-style version of the app to swap between performance modes, change resolution, etc. The button on the right-hand side opens the full-fat Predator Sense app, where you can get more granular with your customisation.

Though it's effectively the same setup as the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X, it's slower and more cumbersome. That seems to be the prevailing truth of pretty much any Windows-based handheld right now.

I notice next to no difference between the 25W Quiet Mode and 30W Balanced Mode, with mere minutes being between them in the PC Mark 10 battery life gaming test.

However, Panther Lake's battery-saving mode (thanks to what Intel calls Endurance Gaming) is truly great, providing just under three hours of battery life. For less intensive use cases, I could see much better battery life. This Endurance mode can be flicked between three different modes, with one end bringing down power for better battery life, and the other bringing that power up in exchange for less battery life. The middle Balanced Mode is how I would use the handheld day-to-day.

The only downside here is that the very lightest mode on the Atlas 8 is currently 25 W, which is the max on Z2 Extreme handhelds while unplugged. You can push that down below 25 W, but you have to set a custom wattage, which I'd wager many handheld owners don't want to mess with. For most, you will be using this between 25 W and 35 W day-to-day.

Recorded using PCMark 10's gaming battery life test (Asus only goes up to 25 W unplugged but Acer goes up to 35 W)

Recorded using PCMark 10's gaming battery life test (Asus only goes up to 25 W unplugged but Acer goes up to 35 W)

Other than its fairly pretty face buttons, the Atlas 8 is a rather plain all-black gaming handheld. It goes without much intricate detailing (other than the Acer Predator RGB logo on the back and RGB rings around the thumbsticks).

As far as the display is concerned, you aren't getting any sort of fancy OLED here, but you do get a genuinely quite bright (500 nits) 16:10 WUXGA IPS display with Corning Gorilla Glass, making it decent in high-light environments. Importantly, I managed to play this out and about, and in front of a window, and could actually make out the game on screen, which is solid.

As of right now, it seems like the only model of the Atlas 8 with a G3 Extreme chip that sells in America comes with 512 GB of storage. That means you are getting half the storage and 75% of the memory of the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ CG3EM for 72% of the cost. But, as far as performance is concerned, I got pretty much identical stats, even beating out the Claw in 3DMark and losing in storage performance. That extra 8 GB of memory is unlikely to provide a major uplift in games, though the extra storage will certainly come in handy. My money would be on the Atlas 8 here.

Then, for the same price, one could pick up the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (or the X for $300 less). Asus has the edge in ergonomics, look, thermals, screen, and storage capacity, but the G3 Extreme is a beast of a chip, handily handing Asus its butt in games. If you have got to pay upwards of $1,000 on a handheld right now, there's actually a good argument to be made for all three devices, though the Atlas 8 offers the best performance-to-price ratio.

It's a shame that Acer has to make little compromises to get that price down, but for $1,300, you will not get a better-performing gaming handheld in my book, and that's still quite impressive.

3. Best high performance: MSI Claw 8 EX AI+

Time marches onward, unyielding and unflinching. Somehow, Skyrim, the latest of the Elder Scrolls games, is now 15 years old. Yes, if it was a child, it'd be going through a moody phase right now, making questionable fashion choices and listening to music that seems expressly designed to annoy you.

On November 11, 2011, The Elder Scrolls 5 came out to a rabid audience of fantasy and RPG fans. Bethesda marked the fact it's somehow been a decade-and-a-half since then with some new artwork. I know, I'm surprised it's not another port too.

On social media, the studio posted a fresh image of a dragonborn facing a giant dragon. It's a bespoke piece of work to commemorate the occasion, created by Karl Fitzgerald, a well-travelled artist who's done a cavalcade of fantastical pieces, including a number around The Lord of the Rings, making him an ideal candidate.

On this day 15 years ago The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim was released. Since that day the community has continued to grow into something truly special. Thank you for being a part of it. This beautiful artwork was created by legendary artist Karl Fitzgerald to mark the occasion. #Skyrim15November 11, 2026

"On this day 15 years ago The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim was released," writes the company. "Since that day the community has continued to grow into something truly special. Thank you for being a part of it."

Fitzgerald's work here is striking. I love the shading, it really makes the fire pop. Some other recent pieces of his include a concert poster for Foo Fighters and newer designers for Pan's Labyrinth and The Wicker Man. It's all gorgeous to look at, imbued with an old school sense of fantasy and adventure.

To me, this feels like it'd be a strong cover for a Skyrim novelization. Which is me basically saying I'd consider a print if they did a run. There was some chatter about a potential announcement from Bethesda to mark the enduring role-playing game being in its mid-teens, but since we just got the title of The Elder Scrolls 6 as part of the industry giant's 40th anniversary celebration, I suspect we'll be waiting before a substantial update comes around.

In the meantime, Skyrim is up to 80% off across all platforms right now. If you're already familiar, it might be time for a new file.

#3995. It looks like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 had fewer active players at launch in the US compared to last year's Black Ops 7

It's been speculated for a while that Call of Duty may be losing its lustre. Although we don't have concrete data with detailed statistics for each game released in the last several years, there's an observable trend in player numbers that's hard to ignore.

US market analysis firm Circana published some data showing player engagement with Modern Warfare 4 following its launch, and compared them to those by Black Ops 7.

The data is based on Circana's proprietary Player Engagement Tracker, which tracks player activity in the US across Steam and PlayStation, and worldwide on Xbox. According to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, 19 percent of players on PlayStation played Modern Warfare 4 in the week ending 24th October, compared to 17 percent on Xbox, and 4.2 percent on Steam.

With the exception of Steam, those numbers are down compared to last year's Black Ops 7, which saw 23 percent engagement on PlayStation, 29 percent on Xbox, and a meagre 1.5 percent on Steam during its launch week.

Call of Duty managed to land in the top 10 across all three platforms during the same week ending 24th October, per Circana. In fact, it sat just below Fortnite on PlayStation, which is a decent result.

The large drop in activity on Xbox could be explained by Modern Warfare 4's lack of a day-one release on Game Pass. Black Ops 7 was the second (and last) Call of Duty to launch on Game Pass day-and-date with its premium release. Game Pass availability typically boosts player numbers, though not always sales.

The drop on PlayStation is a little harder to explain, but could be a side effect of the incredibly successful Black Ops 1 & 2 ports released in the summer on PS4 and PS5, which captured lapsed players who may have simply lost interest in modern Call of Duty, regardless of the perceived quality of Modern Warfare 4.

Judging by the data we have access to, such as SteamDB numbers showing Modern Warfare 4's launch compared to Black Ops 7's and other recent releases, there's evidence this year's game perhaps isn't as popular as it could've been.

Indeed, even Activision's tenor when talking about Call of Duty first weekend sales has changed. The publisher issued a single statement following Modern Warfare 4's launch, through Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, which does not even mention the game by name.

"One of the most celebrated Call of Duty games in its 24-year history, and now $40bn in lifetime franchise revenue," Sharma wrote on X. "An incredible milestone. Congrats to the Activision team. And to the players, thank you for being with us."

Last year's Black Ops 7 post-launch statement sidestepped talk of sales and revenue entirely, insteading praising the "great response to the quality and depth of gameplay in Black Ops 7".

#3994. Terrific fantasy RPG Queen's Domain gets first proper update, adding a new throwing weapon and options to make puzzles "less frustrating"

Extremely good King's Field-style RPG Queen's Domain – or is it a Metroid Prime homage? Or a stealth Morrowind-up? We hacks simply cannot decide – has received its first proper patch, adding a hitherto "missing" throwing weapon, the Grave Knife, alongside a bunch of quality-of-life fixes.

They've stirred in the ability to disable screenshake, alongside some new icons to make status effects more obvious. They've also introduced "options to make some late game puzzles less frustrating", though they don't specify which. How frustrating! Still, it's a tidy overhaul for a game that has rapidly become one of my 2026 favourites.

The big mystery with the update is what the new Grave Knife does. You'll find it inside the Tower of Knowledge, once you've managed to unlock passage. As for those overly aggravating late game puzzles – I find the toughest part of puzzling in Queen's Domain is often just spotting switches and key objects, so perhaps it's something to do with that?

True, there's a large selection of skeleton tableaus who comically point the way to your next objectives, but the game's pixel aesthetics can be rather dense. I very much approve of this on the whole. I like how organic and tumbledown the environment feels - the repeated delight of realising that, yes, you can get over there, and wow, there's a whole other level down here.

Queen's Domain has earned a lot of happy reactions, and is a solid commercial hit. Developers Freshly Baked say it has sold over 100,000 copies, with Vertical Slice reporting that they've already broken even. Glad tidings indeed. Find the full patch notes below, via Steam.

#3993. Guide: PlayStation Studios: All Sony First-Party Developers and What They're Working On

Sony's first-party developers are known collectively as PlayStation Studios, and it's these teams that make all the games published by the company.

Whether it's PS5, PC, or beyond, there are always new games in the works. While we don't always know everything about what's in development, we've done our best to collate all the current info in this page.

Below, you'll find a list of every subsidiary studio under Sony's umbrella as well as what they're currently working on. We'll be updating this article every so often, when new information comes to light.

On this page: PlayStation Studios: All Sony First-Party Developers and What They're Working On

Here are all of Sony's teams working out of the company's home country.

Originally an internal development unit named Polys Entertainment, Polyphony Digital is best known for creating Sony’s flagship racing simulation franchise, Gran Turismo.

Current Projects: Polyphony has been supporting Gran Turismo 7 consistently since launch, with lots of free updates adding new events and vehicles. While this looks set to continue, we expect work has begun on the studio's next game, which will presumably be another Gran Turismo.

Team Asobi rose from the ashes of Japan Studio, initially an internal group building tech demos and on-boarding software such as The Playroom. It brought us Astro Bot Rescue Mission for PSVR, PS5 pack-in game Astro's Playroom, and is now best known for its full-fledged 3D platformer, Astro Bot.

Current Projects: Team Asobi's post-launch updates and support for Astro Bot appears to have concluded, so we can presume the whole studio is now working on its next game. It isn't known what that game is, though given Astro's success, we reckon a sequel is likely.

Below you'll find details on all of SIE's European studios.

Firesprite has an interesting history; it was initially formed by developers from Studio Liverpool, an old Sony studio shuttered in 2012. After The Persistence and supporting Sony on The Playroom and The Playroom VR, it made Horizon Call of the Mountain alongside Guerrilla. It's now SIE's largest UK-based studio.

Current Projects: Firesprite is currently working on Until Dawn 2, a narrative horror adventure game coming to PS5 in January 2027.

Creators of the Killzone franchise, and acquired by Sony following the release of Shellshock: ‘Nam 67 in 2005. One of SIE's most technically capable studios, it's now best known for Horizon Zero Dawn, which runs on the studio's own Decima Engine.

Current Projects: Guerrilla is currently making Horizon Hunters Gathering, a co-op action game with roguelike elements and a very different art style. Also in the works is Horizon Steel Frontiers, an MMO being built for PC and mobile; NCSOFT is spearheading production, but Guerrilla is involved as well. It can also be safely assumed that Horizon 3 is in the pipeline.

Finnish developer Housemarque has worked closely with Sony for over a decade. The studio specialises in arcade-like action, bringing us titles such as Super Stardust HD, Resogun, and of course its latest work, Returnal. The success of the latter pushed Sony to acquire the team in 2021.

Current Projects: Housemarque recently released Saros, a rogue-lite third-person action game that builds on the Returnal formula. It has since released a free update adding more content and features. Plans for what comes next are unknown.

The makers of the LittleBigPlanet franchise, and one of Sony’s most imaginative studios. Media Molecule was acquired by Sony in 2010 following the success of Sackboy’s inaugural adventure.

Current Projects: With post-launch support of Dreams now concluded, Media Molecule is working on its next project, which will be a new IP. It's expected this will reduce the focus on creation and will be a more traditional game. Reports suggest it's making an Animal Crossing-esque life sim.

A company held aloft for its uniformly excellent PC ports, Sony acquired Nixxes in 2021 for this exact purpose. It's mostly been focused on porting existing PlayStation Studios titles to PC, but made its first real creative effort with Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered in 2024.

Current Projects: Nixxes collaborated with Housemarque on Saros. It's also likely to be working on unannounced PC ports.

XDEV is a team that mostly concerns itself with providing support to external teams that are making PlayStation-exclusive titles. Over the years it has helped bring many games to PS5 and PS4, such as Detroit: Become Human, Returnal, Death Stranding, Stellar Blade, Rise of the Ronin, and many others. Though it originated in the UK, the company now also operates in the US and Japan.

Current Projects: XDEV is working with Housemarque on Saros, Arc System Works on Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, and presumably more yet to be announced.

Most of Sony's best-known studios hail from the United States. Here they all are — plus a bonus Canada team!

Infamously created Bubsy 3D for the PS1 before moving on to the Syphon Filter series under the Eidetic name. Acquired by Sony in 2000. Historically focused on portable games, the team broke back into AAA territory with Days Gone on PS4.

Current Projects: Unknown, though reportedly it won't be a Days Gone sequel.

Famed for its expertise in first-person shooters, Bungie has made some of gaming's best-loved franchises in Halo and Destiny. Thanks to its work on the latter, Sony acquired the company in 2022 during its big push into multiplayer and live service games. Bungie has retained some autonomy under this new ownership, though this has softened over time.

Current Projects: Bungie's latest is Marathon, a reinvention of its own sci-fi shooter series from the 90s. This iteration is an intense extraction shooter that launched in March 2026. It'll be supporting this game for the foreseeable future.

A new studio co-founded by Jade Raymond, famed for her work on the Assassin's Creed and Watch Dogs series. The developer has yet to release a game, but has been scooped up by Sony as the team works on its debut project.

Current Projects: Haven was developing the now-cancelled Fairgames, an online multiplayer shooter described as a "competitive heist experience". The studio is currently acting in a support role for other teams.

Famed for PlayStation exclusive series such as Ratchet & Clank and Resistance, the developer has felt like part of the first party family all along. With Marvel's Spider-Man and Marvel's Spider-Man: Miles Morales being such huge hits, it's no wonder Sony scooped the studio up in 2019.

Current Projects: Insomniac recently released Marvel's Wolverine exclusively for PS5 in September 2026. It's extremely likely that Marvel's Spider-Man 3 is in the works, too.

Perhaps the most famous of Sony’s studios, Naughty Dog has a long history creating series such as Crash Bandicoot, Jak & Daxter, Uncharted, and The Last of Us. Acquired in 2001.

Current Projects: Naughty Dog is currently working on sci-fi action adventure game Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet. It's expected this will launch in 2027, though no release information has been announced yet.

Most famous for the critically acclaimed MLB The Show series, San Diego Studio has previously operated as a support studio for external developers, and has also worked on titles like The Mark of Kri and Pain.

Current Projects: San Diego Studio recently launched MLB The Show 26, the latest instalment in its annual series. It's also working on MLB The Show Mobile.

Creators of the God of War franchise. Previously incubated developers like thatgamecompany, while also serving as a support studio for external developers working on exclusive games.

Current Projects: Santa Monica Studio's next game is God of War Laufey, a game following Faye and what happens to her after she dies at the start of God of War (2018). This is due for release in May 2027. Additionally, the team has announced God of War Trilogy Remake, which revisits the Greek mythology games, though this is further out.

One-time Nintendo 64 developer, Sucker Punch is the creator of PlayStation fan favourites like Sly Cooper and inFAMOUS. Acquired by Sony in 2011, the studio is now best known for Ghost of Tsushima.

Current Projects: Sucker Punch most recently released Ghost of Yotei, an indirect sequel to Ghost of Tsushima. Ghost of Yotei Legends, a co-op multiplayer DLC, is now also available. It's unknown what the studio's next game will be.

One of Sony's newest studios, teamLFG is a developer that began as a standalone team within Bungie, but has now spun out to become its own thing. It has yet to release a game.

Current Projects: teamLFG is working on something currently known as Project Gummybears. It's described as a "team-based action game that draws inspiration from fighting games, platformers, MOBAs, life sims, and frog-type games" set within a "lighthearted" and "comedic" sci-fi universe.

Valkyrie is perhaps best known for its GUNS UP! series, which Sony published on various platforms prior to the acquisition. After being a reliable external collaborator on several projects, Valkyrie Entertainment was brought into PlayStation Studios in December 2021. It has since provided support on numerous games including God of War Ragnarok, The Last of Us Part II Remastered, and Uncharted: Legacy of Thieves Collection.

Current Projects: Valkyrie Entertainment holds its cards very close to its chest, so it's difficult to know what it's working on. It can be assumed it's helping out across various projects within PlayStation Studios.

That's everything we know about PlayStation Studios and its current projects. Which is your favourite of Sony's first-party developers? What games do you want to see them make next? Discuss in the comments section below.

As the Editor of Push Square, Sammy has over 15 years of experience analysing the world of PlayStation, from PS3 through PS5 and everything in between. He’s an expert on PS Studios and industry matters, as well as sports games and simulators. He also enjoys RPGs when he has the time to dedicate to them, and is a bit of a gacha whale.

If I had to rank the top five Sony developers in terms of what I’ve seen in terms of fun, graphically and/or technologically impressive games along with potential for future awesomeness:

1. Naughty Dog. It’s been the juggernaut, top dog, tour de force studio that Microsoft’s always dreamt of having, and it’s what Rare should’ve/would’ve been if MS hadn’t wasted Rare’s time with avatars and Kinect experiences.

2. Insomniac. Ratchet and Clank. Spiderman. Spyro. Yeah, Insomniac rules. Here’s hoping for a Feral Rights sequel/remake for PSVR 2, done with the size, scope, and budget a true AAA game should have! Make the system seller VR2 truly needs and deserves. Put our faith back into VR, Sony (or send the job over to MediaMolecule because they’re known for their innovative tech-based PlayStation games.

3. Santa Monica Studios. God of War. Boom!

4. Sucker Punch. InFAMOUS 2 was so, so good! After years of trying different open world games, InFAMOUS 2 was the first one that I truly sunk my teeth into. It was my personal gateway to an entirely new gaming world. And the ability within that game to create and design your own missions? Revolutionary! SP took a slight step back with InFAMOUS: Second Son and First Light, but their work in creating Sly Cooper keeps them at #3.

4. Housemarque. Fantastic action games. In an alternate universe where arcades still exist, Housemarque would be #1 and it wouldn’t even be close.

5. Guerrilla Games. Killzone. Horizon. Awesome-sauce.

As an aside, I love ClapHanz for the fantastic Hot Shots Golf games (which includes the VR game, too!). It’s a pity Sony didn’t pony up the bucks to buy the studio. I’d have loved to see more Hot Shots entries in golf and other sports—tennis, baseball, football, basketball, soccer, volleyball, fencing, curling, hockey, tee-ball, tag, axe throwing, log cutting, fencing, corn detasseling—heck, it doesn’t matter what sports are represented. If it’s done by ClapHanz, it’s good.

@Oram77 Yeah, I didn’t intend to cast any blame or criticism, per se, rather more of a surprising (and disappointing) observation. It is what it is. Development takes ages now. Added to that the poor strategic planning that resulted in several cancelled projects and studio closures and… here we are.

I don’t hold it against Bluepoint or Media Molecule necessarily. It’s just crazy to think they might go the length of the entire generation without a release (Demon’s Souls Remake at launch notwithstanding). I’m sure BluePoint’s PS6 game will be fantastic. And I suspect Mm will squeeze out something on PS5, and it will probably be good too.

The development cycles for even studios that didn’t have years wasted on a canceled project are now around 5-6 years (Taking Ghost of Yotei as an example. Or Death Stranding 2) whereas it was previously about 2 years, especially for sequels. (Again using Sucker Punch as an example — Infamous 2009, Infamous 2 2011, Infamous: Festival of Blood 2011, Infamous Second Son 2014, Infamous First Light 2014.)

I’m not saying anything we don’t already know, development times have increased 2-4x compared to prior generations. It’s one reason why AI may not be such a bad thing as a tool to streamline some of the tasks of development, so long as it doesn’t replace the creative parts of the process. If it can improve efficiency and keep production on track (and keep a studio from being shut down as a result) then maybe that’s a good thing. But that’s a whole other discussion for debate.

I will say also, that despite the drastic ballooning of game development times, there has been an equally significant expansion in number of developers producing games, particularly from emerging markets. As a result there is no shortage of games to play and in fact, we have more games than ever before to choose from. So I don’t necessarily want to imply that it’s doom and gloom.

#3992. I just found out you can use your Steam Wishlist to search for deals on games outside of Steam, saving my nephew more than £40 on Total War: Warhammer 3

It earned me a bucketload of uncle points

I may be very late to the party with this discovery, but I only just realised you can connect your Steam Wishlist to a third-party deals tracker. The beauty of which is that, once hooked up, you can see what games you've been pining for are going cheap not just on Steam but through any major shopfront across the internet.

I worry that I will be coming across as 'Use this one trick to save money – greengrocers hate it!', but it's already helped save my nephew more than £40. Even if it meant using a slightly underhand method.

Two weeks ago, I got a text from my nephew asking what the best way to play Total War: Warhammer 3. When I messaged back a couple of hours later (look, I'm not a responsive uncle) to tell him it's currently £50 on Steam, but it's worth waiting because according to SteamDB's price history it's come down to £7.50 in the past, I was too late. He'd got itchy feet and bought it at full whack on Steam, using up all his birthday money.

That's when I went looking and found Is There Any Deal for the first time. (A lot of you in the comments may be throwing your hands up in despair to hear this oversight) If you've not come across it before, it's a site that tracks game sales across loads of shops, including Steam, EA Store, Epic Games Store, GamersGate, GOG. GreenManGaming, Humble. This means while a game may not be on sale on Steam you can see if it's on sale anywhere else.

In the case of Total War: Warhammer 3, while it was full price on Steam, over on the Humble Store it was discounted to £7.49. I sent a link to my nephew and then told him, using the authority only an uncle has, that it's okay to refund the game through Steam and buy the cheaper version. It's not something I've ever done myself, but he's 17 and that is a lot of money to save.

Anyway, that's recommendation the first. It was only when I was looking for a way to export my Steam Wishlist to ask RPS supporters what I should cull that I realised Is There Any Deal has another feature: you can import every game on your Wishlist to get deal notifications. (This may get a second groan of despair in the comment section.) Once linked up, the site will ping you a notification whenever games you're waiting for pop up in a deal.

Just looking at my current list, I can get Genesis Noir, Ancient Enemy, and Norco for £10 total, all of which with more than 70% discounts through stores other than Steam. So, as you can see, this could be both a saving technically and lead me to spending a lot more money than I mean to…

You may already have heard of these tools, but as I hadn't I thought it best to give them a shout out.

Now considering I've revealed myself to be a rube, what other third party tools should I be installing to weaponise my Steam Library?

#3991. Indie game website itch.io expands its AI disclosure filter as 'AI slop' continues to overwhelm Steam and other storefronts

Indie game storefront itch.io has expanded its AI disclosure filters, allowing its users to better separate games made with the controversial technology from those who don't.

This expansion, revealed on its official BlueSky account, includes Itchio's search page which now features a "No AI" box. By ticking this, users can hide any game on the website that features the generative AI disclosure. Games created using generative AI must have this disclosure to be present on the platform, similarly to Steam, although without an option to describe to what extent the tech was used.

This change comes shortly after itch.io also revealed the number of game pages being made on the website each day had doubled in the past two months. And, of course, the number of games downloaded and purchases have not doubled to match this new supply.

itch.io is also facing issues linked to the sheer file size. The storefront has a terms of service policy against AI spam, which it cited shortly after it publicly announced "a couple terabytes of AI slop" had been deleted.

This change comes as the industry as a whole has been clogged with an influx of AI games. Steam Next Fest had a record-breaking number of demo submissions last month. Developers pulled demos in fear of their game being copied, and with Steam saying it's the developer's responsibility to make their games less copyable.

It's an issue that isn't going away any time soon. Even as Claude creator Anthropic has introduced rules preventing unoriginal game clones, alternative AI tools can still be used to create them, and the process of creating games using AI tools will still allow for hastily made, low effort slop. Perhaps filters, like the one itch.io has expanded, is a workable solution to this on-going problem.

I really wasn't expecting Microsoft Paint to turn up in the cybersecurity headlines, but here we are. MS disclosed and patched a security vulnerability within the software on October 13, but it's worth checking your own Paint version to see if you've received the update.

Some users don't have automatic Microsoft Store updates enabled, especially those on work machines. As Paint is updated via the store, you may need to manually update to version 11.2609.401.0 to keep your machine secure.

To confuse things further, International Cyber Digest reports that the MS store was providing older versions to some users until recently, and Windows Latest didn't seem to receive the new version even with auto updates enabled. Or, there's been some mixup with release numbers. It's genuinely difficult to tell at this point, with differing information coming from multiple sources.

The vulnerability was initially given an 8.1 severity rating on the CVSS scale, but Microsoft downgraded it to a 7.0 score on November 9 according to Threat Defence. MS also changed its description of the bug to that of a local exploit (requiring a user to open a crafted file) rather than a network attack vector, .

Regardless, to check whether your Paint version is hopefully up-to-date (what a world we live in), open the app, go to the Settings menu, and check the version number beneath the "About Paint" section. If it's lower than version 11.2609.401.0, open the Microsoft Store and manually update the app. Or, if your Windows 11 settings don't allow user updates, contact your sysadmin.

You can also check your Paint version within Windows Powershell by running:

Honestly, this is the biggest omnishambles of conflicting cybersecurity info I've seen in a while. Some outlets initially reported the bug as a no-click security flaw, while others have suggested that the vulnerability could potentially be exploited via a specially crafted image. Microsoft shifting the security goalposts as it goes really hasn't helped, nor has its apparently messy roll out of the patched version.

Anyway, it's still worth checking if Paint has been updated, folks. One way or another, we'll get to the bottom of this eventually. Or we'll just keep updating every aspect of our machines on a tediously regular basis, in the hope that some of these messy leak-plugging antics might do some good.

And Rockstar's institutional knowledge is "absolutely priceless"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rockstar's ability to create world-beating titles like GTA 6 stems from a core practice - not succumbing to the 'fire and rehire' cycle that has ravaged publishers like Microsoft and Sony.

That's according to David O'Reilly, a 12-year veteran of Rockstar whose credits as an environment artist cover GTA 6, Red Dead Redemption 2, GTA 5. He claims that "Rockstar doesn't do the whole thing that the games industry has been madly scrambling to do" over the past few years - namely, laying off vast swathes of staff to cut costs, before scaling back up when production needs require doing so.

"How does Rockstar do it?" he asks. "How are they performing these magical feats of game development? It's pretty simple really: They've not engaged in that fire/rehire cycle." The result, O'Reilly claims, is that "Rockstar has kept nearly all of its institutional knowledge," and that in his time at the studio he worked alongside people who had been at Rockstar North when it was still known as DMA Design, a rebrand that took place in early 2002.

That heritage, he says, "is a big deal in today's gaming industry," and the associated "knowledge bank" that comes with keeping your long-serving staff around is invaluable. It's also something that "Sony, Microsoft, all these big publishers [...] don't understand, because they're focused on the money. They don't give a crap about making games. Make no mistake - they do not care about making game products."

That apathy is something O'Reilly believes even Take-Two, Rockstar's long-standing publisher, shares. The difference is that the company recognises "that Rockstar is a Golden Goose," and remains very hands-off with the development studio "because they're terrified of breaking something in that winning formula. [...] They let Rockstar cook their good stuff, and it's worked for a long time and it's continuing to work."

O'Reilly's position - that a short-term approach of firing and rehiring does nothing to actually help a studio - is certainly one that's beginning to be vindicated. After thousands of layoffs and dozens of studio closures across the industry over recent years, the idea we're getting better games as a result is laughable. In fact, the opposite is true - in the past, plenty of classics were made because the teams that made the first game all stuck around to improve the sequel. And just this week, Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma pointed out that the Ocarina of Time remake owes some of its success to the fact Nintendo doesn't engage in mass layoffs.

Perhaps his claim - that "noone is competing with Rockstar" - is not entirely fair. For one thing, there are studios out there that are widely retaining talent and are continuing to push out acclaimed games. For another, Rockstar's resource - fuelled by billions in GTA 5 revenue - is literally world-beating. But maybe you can't really put a figure on it - as O'Reilly says: At Rockstar, you have a lot of people who have been there 20 years or more, [...] and that sort of knowledge is absolutely priceless.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

#3988. Intergalactic PS5 in the 'Last Stage of Production', Gameplay Coming Next Year

Neil Druckmann thinks the game will "surprise people"

Since the announcement of Naughty Dog's next big game, Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, we really haven't seen or heard much about it. In 2027, though, that's set to change.

In a brief appearance on a live show at Comic Creators Block Party 2026, director Neil Druckmann has teased a few things about the upcoming sci-fi adventure.

You can see all the Intergalactic chatter in the post below:

Druckmann says the game is at the "last stage of production", meaning "we can play it, we're refining and polishing it". He says he "can't wait to show it to the world."

It sounds like 2027 will be big for Intergalactic, as Sony and Naughty Dog will "show a lot of it next year" including "gameplay" and "more of the story". Whether the game actually launches next year is another question, but at the very least we'll be seeing plenty more of it.

"I think it'll really surprise people, what they think the game is and what it actually is," Druckmann says.

He also talks about how Naughty Dog has been making "relatively grounded" games for a long time with Uncharted and The Last of Us, and Intergalactic presents an opportunity for the team to explore something more fantastical.

"Something we've been really hungry for is to go sci-fi," he says, referring to the studio's previous series, Jak & Daxter.

"We really wanted to take everything we learned from that franchise, which is sci-fi/fantasy, the pulp action adventure stuff we learned with Uncharted, the more serious drama we got from The Last of Us... [Intergalactic] really is a combination of those three franchises."

Druckmann continues, talking about how the aim is to combine Naughty Dog's cinematic storytelling chops with "deeper gameplay systems" in Intergalactic.

I'm super excited to finally learn more about this game in 2027; fingers crossed its release won't be too far behind.

#3987. Real-time strategy game The Fertile Crescent 2 is an isometric odyssey inspired by Age of Empires, with the 1.0 release out now

Time to power-rank the biggest Bronze Age civs

Age of Empires-influenced real-time strategy game The Fertile Crescent 2: Collapse of the Bronze Age leaves early access today, publishers MicroProse have announced, with the 1.0 version adding the final chapters of the singleplayer story. You'll also get your grubby fingers on the very same map editor developers Wield Interactive used to design the campaign.

I'm new to The Fertile Crescent 2 myself. I do like the sound of a strategy sim in which you guide a fugitive community through the Late Bronze Age Collapse. The land has been thrown into turmoil by the arrival of the Sea People, this being a loose historical term for assorted ocean-going migrants who, I gather, are often blamed for the crumbling of the Hittites among other once-glorious Bronze Age powers. I don't have much scholarly insight to share - I thought the "Sea People" referred to expansionist mermaids, at first - but I do have a trailer.

Nate Crowley (RPS in peace) was exceedingly fond of the original game, calling it "a bite-sized chunk of phenomenal RTS design" that "manages to riff nostalgically on Age Of Empires, while completely rewriting its ground rules". The sequel continues with the same core concepts – above all, the paramount importance of food, which determines population and army size together with your civ's progression.

"This is not a game about building the biggest empire," the developers explain in a press release. "Resources have to be managed, stability is fragile, and growth comes with risk. Every expansion, every battle, and every decision must be weighed against survival. Building and managing a sustainable economy is as important as commanding your forces in battle. Expanding your army too quickly can put your food economy under pressure."

The story spans 17 missions, with four playable factions: the Assyrians, Egyptians, Babylonians, and Hittites. The 1.0 release also includes some standalone scenario missions, a skirmish mode, and multiplayer on dedicated servers with bot support.

Read more on Steam. If you're partial to historical strategy and don't mind winding back the clock (upturning the hourglass? Adjusting the sundial? Recalibrating the henge?) another few thousand years, Folk Emerging is pretty terrific. If you like stories about migrant tribes, and you don't mind trading your Hittites for Vikings, you might get a kick out of The Banner Saga.

#3986. COD: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ patch has nerfed UAV Towers so you're not immediately visible everywhere you go

The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 patches continue, with the latest delivering some big changes to the game's extraction mode DMZ. The latest hotfix introduced a key balance change to one of DMZ's most controversial mechanics: UAV Towers.

UAV Towers, previously guaranteed to spawn in every Point of Interest (POI) in the map, have now had their spawn logic randomised. Infinity Ward also reduced their spawn rate by 40 percent, meaning you're less likely to find them across the various regions of the map. As noted in the patch notes, that change also prevents multiple towers from spawning the same area. The only exception is the Deadtown area, which factors into DMZ Order progression and requires multiple towers.

By taking away the guarantee that each POI will have at least one UAV Tower, the patch removes one of the core tactics PvP-inclined and aggressive players have been relying on since DMZ's launch. It's common for players to spawn in, and immediately run around activating as many UAV Towers as possible to reveal the movement of enemy players, even if they're not interested in directly engaging them.

Indeed, some of the UAV Towers cover extraction areas, so it's easy for players intending to ruin the day of others as they're extracting to set up elaborate traps. Making matters worse, a particular character trait prevents UAV Towers from expiring, allowing the scans to stay up for the entire match.

Infinity Ward has not commented directly on that trait, but the developer confirmed it's being changed so the Sedative Inhaler - which hides you from UAVs - also works with those trait-upgraded towers, though that change won't arrive until sometime in Season 1.

Finally, today's update further makes it easier to stay undetected by boosting the Sedative Inhaler's duration to 120 seconds, double that of the previous 60, which should help while we wait for larger changes to be implemented.

I'll be the first to admit I've said some incredibly questionable-sounding things while playing videogames. Or talking about them in public. But I would like to think that the one place where I would be extra careful about the words coming out of my mouth are in an airport, or on an airplane. Really, anywhere with an insane amount of security and an ever-pervasive fear of anything explosives-related.

Unfortunately, for passengers on board a Frontier Airlines flight earlier this week, however, one such gamer was not so cautious. As reported by CBS News, one plane at California's Ontario International Airport had to be evacuated over a bomb scare, only for it to be some guy playing Call of Duty with his pal.

According to reports, one passenger overheard words such as "bomb" and "explosion" and, rightly so, went and told staff about it. The situation led to both the plane and the east wing of Terminal 2 being evacuated, and a check of the aircraft which revealed that no explosives or bombs were on board.

After detaining and speaking to the culprit, it was revealed that he was, in fact, on FaceTime with his buddy while playing Call of Duty together. He was released without any charges, and the flight was reboarded and departed later that night.

I do feel a little bad for laughing about it—as a nervous flyer, I know for a fact that if I had been that passenger overhearing the conversation I may very well have gone into full-blown panic mode. I don't even like when someone doesn't put their phone on airplane mode as we're taking off!

But I'm also the type of person to watch my friend's Discord streams while I'm out and about, and I honestly dread to think about the kind of things passerbys have heard me say while spectating games. Hell, I'm sure even my neighbours have heard some absurd sentences leave my mouth when I've been raiding in Final Fantasy 14 with the windows wide open. If you're reading this neighbours, I'm sorry.

#3984. What are we all playing this weekend?

This is the last empty weekend before I go on holiday for a frankly indulgent three weeks. As such, it will likely be spent either remembering all the things my partner and I've not organised for the time we're away or racing to clear through the pile of things I've already remembered I've not organised for the holiday. Whatever the case, it shall not be restful.

Where am I going? Let's just say, I hope to return with some new pairs of glasses and a pair of trainers. If that doesn't give it away, I don't know what will.*

Now, this is what the rest of the team are up to.

EdwinI'm embroiled in helping with a house move again this weekend, so there will be precious little gaming for me. I'd like to fit in a bit more Queen's Domain. I'm happy that the game appears to have caused a stir.

JeremyCastlevania work continues this weekend for our walkthrough, but I'm nearing the finish line. As my anxiety has been pretty bad lately, I will also do my best to catch up on sleep and enjoy time with the wife, as we're both having a very busy end-of-the-year. Dim sum on Sunday afternoon will hopefully be nice.

MarkI must keep my lips shut about what I'll be playing for the majority of this weekend, but if I get any time beyond that I'd like to carry on swan diving my way through Assassin's Creed 3's remaster.

James'Video games? I spit on video games!' James said. 'I would not end my week with such nonsense, not when I could be usefully spending time refining my perpetual motion machine.' Sadly, we all know that's a euphemism for sitting in a rocking chair and eating off-brand Doritos.

OllieI'm gonna return to Marathon for a while, I think. I miss the feel of its maps. But I'll probably need something a bit less stressful to play as well, balance it out a bit. CallumMarching toward the Treehouse exit in a suit made of tent canvas, Callum announced he was going camping. His jacket sleeves and trouser legs were lined with tentpoles, which made the sight of him trying to climb down the rope ladder an awkward one.

JulianThis weekend I'm playing games that aren't exactly secret – they're all out in the world and playable – but I need to keep them secret from you. #3983. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is confirmed, finally getting new trailer and full name, 8 years, 4 months, and 23 days after its reveal

Today, Xbox and Bethesda have finally revealed the name and more information about The Elder Scrolls 6. The game, which we now know carries the subtitle Sentinel, was revealed in a special video that took place today, 3rd November 2026, almost exactly 15 years since the launch of The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim and eight years, four months, and 23 days since the first reveal of the title card for The Elder Scrolls 6. That's over 100 months, by the way, or 3067 days, if you want to get specific.

In the trailer, a glimpse of the new game - mostly with some fancy sand physics - before the name, Sentinel, is revealed formally. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate," says a quote in the video, attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell.

"For 40 years, we've explored new worlds, told unforgettable stories, and gone on incredible adventures together," says a blurb for new video. "From everyone at Bethesda Game Studios, thank you for joining us along this journey, for making these worlds your own, and for inspiring us to keep creating. Here's to 40 more."

This reveal comes after a report last week suggested we'd be seeing more of the highly-anticipated fantasy RPG in November, and which also predicted the name of the game. That report suggested that the title will take place in the Tamriel region of Hammerfell, will touch on the "history of the Elder Scrolls" and will "help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts". This trailer seems to confirm all that.

Asha Sharma, CEO of Xbox, said she'd played the game in August on a trip to the Bethesda offices, as a giant inflatable rat and a union protest took place outside. Notably, the reveal of the game is taking place not six months after Bethesda suffered sweeping job cuts (alongside many other Microsoft-owned studios) as part of Xbox's "reset".

So why has it taken eight years for Bethesda to show us this game? Previously, Skyrim's lead designer Bruce Nesmith noted that the studio and boss Todd Howard felt pressured to reveal the game to the world because "the pitchforks and torches were out". "[...] Todd's opinion - one which I share, by the way - is that the video game industry has short memories," he said in an interview in 2023. "Those companies that start touting their games years ahead of time, actually, you know, they screw themselves. The best time to start talking about it is six months before release." It's worth noting, then, that this is what Bethesda did with Fallout 4.

Does that hint at a timeline for more Sentinel footage being shown soon, and a potentially sooner-than-we-thought release date? Who knows. If we are going to see the game again anytime soon, it's most likely going to be during The Game Awards 2026, which is taking place on 10th December.

Nothing zaps the joy right out of launch day celebrations like getting laid off alongside half of your team, but that's exactly what happened to dozens of Id Software developers during Microsoft's July 2026 bloodbath (not to be confused with its September 2026 bloodbath) alongside the release of the Revelations DLC for Doom: The Dark Ages. Amid reports that the studio was gutted down to support studio size, the total confirmed number of laid off employees, per Game Developer, was 136 as of this past July, which current studio leadership has confirmed was about half of the team. That's an absolutely devastating loss of institutional talent, but a group of former Id Software devs has risen from the ashes as new worker-owned studio Hidden Horses. In the studio's announcement documentary, they don't hold back.

"It's just wild the talent that they let go. It's just wild that they would attack Id like that the day before we release our DLC. It really felt like an attack," says Hidden Horses co-founder and former Id Software tools programmer John-Michael Quinlan.

"It was probably emotionally the worst day of my life," says former Id Software senior technical designer Jordan Turner, who's now co-founder and, fittingly, technical designer at Hidden Horses. "I don't think I've cried that much in my entire life."

"I did not see it coming at the time that I was told," says former Id Software programmer, now Hidden Horses rendering programmer, Regan Carver. "I just told my wife, 'well that was not a fun conversation.' She thought I was joking at first, and then she realized I wasn't. I was in shock, but she was in tears.

"I usually spend the release days scouring social media looking for all the good news. It drives up my morale ... I'm always excited to see people receiving our stuff well and knowing I was a small part of it, so that was gone."

Amid a period of historic tumult in the gaming industry, it's easy to become desensitized by news of another mass layoff, but hearing from the workers themselves in this way really underscores the immense human toll of corporate downsizing.

Former Id Software AI engineering lead Daniel Young says the hardest part about being laid off was losing friends he'd worked with for years. "It hit me pretty hard. I think that was the biggest thing was the people that I was gonna be leaving behind. I hate to say it's like a death in the family, but it's almost like that's what it felt like," says Young.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"Personally the biggest thing was that I'm trying to help my kids through college," says Todd Boyce, former Id Software lead VFX artist and Hidden Horses technical artist. "I have two kids in college right now, and that is really expensive. That's probably the thing that hurts me the most is the possibility of them being financially stressed because of something that wasn't even in their control, and for a layoff that honestly didn't need to happen."

Hidden Horses is a small studio of 19 developers according to this announcement video, and its Kickstarter describes its debut title, Danger Pay, as "a single player FPS based around a deadly gameshow with high-octane action and gameplay focused design." Meanwhile, Hidden Horses producer Andrew Willis says players can expect "absolutely stellar out-of-this-world fun gameplay, amazing and super cohesive and stylistic visuals, and really optimized gameplay on the technical side."

Technical designer Tim Locke says one key difference between working at a corporate-owned studio like Id and now Hidden Horses is creative freedom. "Being able to do what we want and talk through, like, what are our ideas, like, which ones resonate with the most people and how do we move forward with that. That's really the difference, and it has been different so far. It's been great."

Echoing that sentiment, Hidden Horses lighting artist Tyler DeLisle says "the people that were let go at Id ... we were all, none of us were slackers. We were all best of the best, top of our game, so now that we're all given this opportunity to come together and keep doing what we love to do, but kind of untethered and more collaborative, I think we can really put out something special."

"If even a small measure of those games that we've worked on in the industry, for me over the past 20 years, is able to be distilled down into a game for our fans, I think they're gonna get something really special," says Quinlan. "And I think you only have to look at the pedigree of the people involved to know that we can do something really special here."

Inside Xbox, "the only concrete thing they have communicated is they want higher profits, and they want it now," says id Software employee

After earning an English degree from ASU, I worked as a corporate copy editor while freelancing for places like SFX Magazine, Screen Rant, Game Revolution, and MMORPG on the side. I got my big break here in 2019 with a freelance news gig, and I was hired on as GamesRadar's west coast Staff Writer in 2021. That means I'm responsible for managing the site's western regional executive branch, AKA my home office, and writing about whatever horror game I'm too afraid to finish.

#3981. New Witcher 3 DLC Uses AI to Touch Up Geralt's Polish Voice Due to Actor's Health Issues

CD Projekt Red has worked with an AI voice generation company on next year's The Witcher 3 expansion, Songs of the Past, so the Polish voiceover for Geralt can match the original game.

Jacek Rozenek, the original Polish voice actor for Geralt has returned to voice the character for all the content in Songs of the Past. However, the actor unfortunately suffered a stroke in recent years that impacted his voice. This has left his voice unrecognisable compared to the lines he recorded for the original RPG.

Having received Rozenek's blessing, CD Projekt Red recorded all his voice work for Songs of the Past, and has taken that work to AI company Respeecher, who will make it sound like Geralt from the base game.

Again, this only affects the Polish language option. Doug Cockle has returned to voice Geralt for the English language version.

Rozenek suffered a stroke in 2019, and he was unable to speak following it. Through hours of training every day, he was able to return to voice acting in 2022, when CD Projekt Red released the PS5 version of The Witcher 3. There was a new quest in that edition, and the work he had to put into the voice lines accompanying it left Rozenek "exhausted" after the recording.

Rozenek has recorded his Polish voice lines for Songs of the Past as usual, but he's supportive of the developer's decision to involve Respeecher to make them sound like Geralt: "The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago. I have great trust... for the creators of this game."

Respeecher has used AI tools trained on Rozenek's previous work as Geralt to match the voices as much as possible.

News Here's 13 Minutes of Witcher 3: Songs of the Past DLC Gameplay

"We basically delivered to Respeecher all the lines that Jacek recorded for us for The Witcher 3,” explained localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed. “They created an algorithm of his voice, based on his lines."

Szwed added that CD Projekt Red only considered this route because of Rozenek's health issues, and having gained his blessing, thinks this is an "ethical" use of AI that can do some good.

Songs of the Past is slated to launch for PS5 at some point in 2027, off the back of the recently released The Witcher 3 Remastered.

#3980. After Star Wars Zero Company dev Bit Reactor brought back an unspecified number of furloughed devs, some of those who weren't have seemingly been laid off

"I’m really proud of what we built together"

Early last month, Star Wars Zero Company developer Bit Reactor brought back a number of developers who had been furloughed before the game launched in August. At the time they did not specify how many devs were returning to the studio, with a separate report claiming more than half had become full time staffers again. Unfortunately, it does now seem like not everyone was able to be brought back, with a number of now former workers sharing word of having been laid off.

As spotted by Star Wars outlet Bespin Bulletin, multiple developers shared word of their layoffs to LinkedIn. A producer at Bit Reactor, Michael Blackard was seemingly one of the first to report being laid off, alongside senior QA analyst Ryan Mosher. Ryan Lopez, an environment artist at the studio, shared, "I was laid off from Bit Reactor this week after a three-month furlough, and while it stings, I’m really proud of what we built together." Lopez had apparently been working on the game for more than three years, starting all the way back on the game's pre-production period.

Tyler Eichten, a UI engineer, also said, "As of today, my time with Bit Reactor has come to a close due to a layoff. I am immensely proud of the work that I, the UI/UX team, and the team at large have accomplished. I hope that in this tumultuous industry that my coworkers (and myself) find placement." It's unclear at this point in time if any, or how many, other staffers have been formally laid off, and Bit Reactor are yet to make a comment.

Star Wars Zero Company performed very well both critically and commercially, making it all the more disappointing that not all of those who worked on the game, who made it as great as it seemingly is, get to continue working at the studio. As always, solidarity with all devs affected.

Per the official Rockstar Games website, Grand Theft Auto 6 will be pre-loadable starting on the 10th November. On PlayStation 5, it'll be available starting at midnight in your local time, but on the Xbox Series X/S, it'll be 12am GMT on the 10th November. On the PlayStation Store you'll need to find the game on the digital store and pre-order the game. On the Xbox Series X/S, the same is true. It goes without saying (yet here I am saying it) that Grand Theft Auto 6 is going to be huge. We don't really have a sense as to just how huge at this point: Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has boasted that GTA 6 preorder numbers are "unprecedented," but he's refused to provide specifics because "the raw numbers could be potentially misleading." But huge, for sure.

Now both Sony and Xbox have joined in the 'gonna be huge' chorus, each of them announcing that preorders for GTA 6 are, definitionally, unprecedented.

"Grand Theft Auto 6 is now the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store," Sony proclaimed on the PlayStation Blog. "Given this unprecedented demand, we’ve joined with Rockstar Games to allow players to start pre-loading the game nine days early, so they’re ready to play on launch day. We’ve also adopted a rolling midnight launch by country, beginning at 12:00AM NZDT in New Zealand and running across the globe as respective countries hit midnight on November 19."

Xbox made a similar announcement on its own website, calling GTA 6 "the most pre-ordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store" and encouraging users to begin preloading as soon as possible because of "the unprecedented demand" for the game.

Alongside Xbox Series X/S consoles, Xbox said GTA 6 will also be playable on Xbox One consoles through Xbox Cloud Gaming. That service is also available on PC, but Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Bell confirmed in October that GTA 6 will not be streamable on our platform.

Today marks the first step in our new 10-year strategic partnership with Take-Two. GTA VI, already the most pre-ordered game ever on Microsoft Store, will be playable on XBOX One through cloud gaming when it launches on November 19.November 10, 2026

But while nobody is serving up specifics on the number of GTA 6 copies sold via preorder, we do have a rough indicator of how much money Take-Two expects to make when it comes out of the gate. The publisher is projecting net bookings of $3.35 to $3.5 billion for its current fiscal quarter, "driven by the groundbreaking release of Grand Theft Auto 6" on November 19. That's roughly double what Take-Two took in during the same quarter in its previous year, when it reported net bookings of $1.76 billion.

"The launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is ten days away and, with pre-orders continuing to reach unprecedented levels, we expect to deliver an historic year for our company," Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick said during yesterday's quarterly financial report.

Take-Two is also projecting a comparably huge net bookings increase for its full year: The company reported total net bookings of $6.72 billion for its 2026 fiscal year, and is currently projecting $8 to $8.2 billion for 2027.
